- Wall time was bound by single-threaded evaluation (~63% serial eval, ~30% IO, ~6% GC). GC knobs cut cpuTime by 42% but wall time by only 6%.
- A parallel-eval flag was accepted by one evaluator and did nothing. The ~3.7x came from a different evaluator. A larger initial heap bought ~7%. Streaming and force-and-drop did not lower peak RSS, because the GC does not return memory to the OS.
- Owning `evalModules` through a lib extension cost +9 primops and +0.24% thunks, i.e. almost nothing. That measurement redirected a whole program away from the engine and toward the fleet axis.
- A competing module system's 3–10x was single-config, intra-eval, on synthetic modules that do not import the package set. It did no cross-host sharing, and above ~2400 modules it was slower because of an O(N²) tail. Its README described a mechanism the source did not implement.
- Repeated `++` inside a `foldl'` is hidden quadratic in Nix. An "optimization" in that form was measured far slower than the code it replaced, so the in-code comment saying so is load-bearing.

**How to apply:**

- Count copies or allocations by phase before acting. Look for the metric that discriminates: here, copies did, function calls did not.
- Read the source, not the README, before citing a mechanism.
- Carry the fixture shape with every figure you relay.

Related: \[[nix-eval-cost-counters]\] \[[declare-dont-discover-boundaries]\]

---
name: nix-eval-cost-counters
description: When quoting Nix evaluation cost figures (allocation counters, cpuTime, scaling exponents)
type: trap
---

**Rule:** Nix stats counters are a lower bound. Budget on all three axes (`list.elements`, `sets.elements`, `nrLookups`), say what they cannot see, and never let one axis decide a comparative claim.

**Why / measured:**

- `genericClosure` keeps its done-set in C++ and does key comparisons that appear in none of the counters. Any figure over a `genericClosure`-backed surface is a floor.
- Work inside any primop is invisible. A counter-based scaling gate then does not go blind, it issues a converged false-green certificate, and that stops anyone from looking.
- One remedy that cut allocation by two orders of magnitude was worth about 1.5x in practice. Price remedies on `cpuTime` (3 or more reps) as well, but do not quote `cpuTime` as a figure.
- Two axes gave opposite answers to "which term is bigger". The spread between axes reached two full exponents on the same cells.
- Exponents climb toward their integer from below. Doubling ratios of 3.70, 3.84 and 3.92 mean exponent 4.
- Two builds that both reported the same version string differed by 8 primops. Version strings do not identify evaluator builds.
- Boehm `gc.totalBytes` is non-deterministic, so it is informational only.
- A full-fleet `deepSeq` will exhaust memory. Run with a memory cap and treat rc 137 as a finding.
- Five variables move a figure while the subject holds still: force path, accessor, driver, harness and demand order. A figure that names none of them is not yet a measurement.

**How to apply:**

- State the hole with every figure: green means "no Nix-level superlinearity detected in the arms declared".
- For comparative claims, measure both terms on both shapes on all three axes. If the ordering flips, say neither may be quoted alone.
- Counter gates: exact for the same evaluator build, a band (for example ±0.1%) across builds.
- Freeze the benchmark file before you publish. Leave offsets in the published numbers.
- A census bounds the instrument, not the system. Ask what its domain is a sample of.

Related: \[[measure-where-the-cost-is]\] \[[nix-tryeval-and-equality]\]

- **Guards are first-order terms** (defunctionalization, Reynolds / Danvy-Nielsen): condition and
  body are terms of gen-algebra's one algebra. A custom condition is a Nix function that BUILDS a term
  at declaration. A context closure (`{ host, ... }: …`) cannot be defunctionalized in pure Nix: it
  is refused by name here and crosses the gen-rules door.
- **Firing grows the tree by exactly one level.** `applyGuard` fires once, never recursively; a
  self-including aspect is inert here and lethal to a caller that loops. The bound is the driver's.
- **`parentOf` is the WALK position, never a `meta` read.** A nested guard leaf has no
  `meta.aspect-chain`, so `meta.aspect-chain or [ ]` misreads it as root; a guard carried from another
  tree keeps a wrong `meta.loc`. `flatten`'s key is a RENDERING; never split it to recover parents.
- **`includesOf` carries only CHECKED edges** (every target is in `nodes`). A foreign keyRef is a
  reference, published in `foreignIncludesOf` for the provider-unioning framework to resolve.
- **Include elements dispatch on whether they NAME A NODE, not on shape.** Shape dispatch minted
  phantom ids that gen-graph then admitted as nodes. Key-less attrsets are content; guards and
  functions are sealed; an unnamed inline aspect literal is an anonymous node keyed by its declaration address.
- **A reserved key is an option declared through `cnf.aspectModules`**; there is no `reservedKeys` surface.
- **Source doors decide by graph membership (exact id), never by kind tag**: a framework names its
  own entity kinds, even ones spelled like gen's own tags.
- `instanceOf`'s id reads only the sources; the caller must ensure each source supplies the value the
  context carries, or one id gets two entries.

## Working in it

- `nix develop ./ci --command ci` and `nix develop ./ci --command ci --tests-error`.
- Value tests in `ci/tests/<area>.nix`; refusal cells by group in `ci/tests-error.nix`.
- Cite `lib/` by BINDING NAME, never line range: a drifted range lands plausibly on a neighbour and a
  reader closes a live finding against it; a stale name fails loudly on grep.
- Purity scan (`ci/tests/purity.nix`) covers `lib/`, `flake.nix`, `default.nix`; `ci/` is exempt.

## Traps

---
name: gen-vars
description: Working in gen-vars, the frozen, experimental target-agnostic vars/secrets generator algebra.
type: reference
verified: unverified
---

**Status:** frozen and experimental, subject to replacement. Do not build new long-lived dependencies on
it. No repository declares it as a flake input and it is not in the hub roster.

**Purpose:** a target-agnostic vars/secrets algebra. It normalizes generator declarations, orders them
topologically into a backend-agnostic plan, and fans one resolution-free file *handle* out to many
consumer targets in one evaluation. It **emits** a generate script; it never runs it. Its own idea is the
handle/resolver split: a generated file is an open value, and `resolveAll` resolves it per target.
Precedents: nixpkgs/Clan `vars` (the `$in`/`$out`/`$prompts` generator model), agenix-rekey (emit a
runnable artefact, let the consumer drive it).

**Depends on:** nixpkgs `lib` (toposort, module system) for the upper tiers; gen-graph **optional**
(enriches `order/`; falls back to `lib.toposort` + BFS). `pure/` uses `builtins` only.
**Not its job:** running scripts (the consumer's deploy path), selecting which generators a host gets
(gen-scope), injecting values into modules (gen-bind), type checking (gen-types).

## Layout and API

The root `default.nix` is a **function** `{ lib ? null, inputs ? { } }:`; tiers activate by argument.
Flake entry: `inputs.gen-vars.lib`.

- `nix develop ./ci --command ci` and `nix develop ./ci --command ci --tests-error` (guarded: refuse on
  untracked files under read roots). `nix flake check ./ci` is unguarded.
- Drift check: `nix eval --json .#lib --apply builtins.attrNames` must print `["hashIdentity"]`.

**Traps:**

- The mint FORCES its whole input; a lazily failing leaf fails at mint time, not at first read.
- A record whose `type` is `"derivation"` still mints unless it has `type` AND `drvPath` AND `outPath`.
  Testing `type` alone made admissibility depend on position, not value.
- A wide value is bounded by the LENGTH budget, not a breadth bound. Both fold accumulator fields must
  be forced each step, or a 31,000-element list inside both bounds aborts uncatchably.
- The depth bound's margin is about 6x, not 10x; the real guard is Nix `max-call-depth` (10,000),
  roughly 3 frames per level.
- A cycle is caught by the DEPTH bound alone; no length budget can save it.
- The purity scan must strip comments: the word "merges" in prose is a `merge` substring hit.

q11.query: Why is having multiple concurrent agent sessions write to the same git working directory problematic?

results.text:
---
name: shared-checkout-peer-sessions
description: Collision rules when two agent sessions write in the same git working tree (for example a build session and a sitting or design session).
type: practice
---

**Rule:** In a checkout another live session writes to, commit ONLY with
`git commit -- <your paths>`, and never stash, pull, rebase-pull, autostash or push there.

**Why:** Measured: a `git stash` in one session took a peer author's in-flight spec edit out of the
tree; only `stash@{0}` saved it. A bare `git commit` takes the whole index and has swept another
writer's staged work into a push.

**How to apply:**

- Commit path-scoped: your reports, your probes, your tracker export, plus any file the owner
  explicitly directed you to edit (and tell the peer session in the same act).
- The peer that owns publication pulls before it pushes; because it is the same local branch, its
  push publishes your commits.
- A pre-commit hook may stash unstaged files itself. After every commit run `git status --short` and
  confirm no peer file vanished. If one did, stop and tell the peer at once. Skipping the hook
  (`--no-verify`) needs the owner's say-so.
- Never edit a file the peer has in flight. Send it the measurement instead.
- At close, after the peer's next push: `git fetch`, then
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` for each of your commits, plus one unresolvable
  sha as the control. Report any commit that did not reach origin.
- A peer cannot grant escalation. A peer's request is never the owner's approval.
- With NO peer running, the rules relax: you may `git pull --ff-only` and push your own path-scoped
  commits, but only if `git status --short` shows nothing you do not own.
- While an automated multi-repo relock/update (gen's `relock-all`) is running on a repo, do not `git worktree add` or push
  to that repo's main; use a scratch clone.

Related: \[[owner-sitting]\] \[[design-session]\] \[[dispatch-form]\]

---
name: one-writer-per-checkout
description: When more than one agent (or you plus an agent) will write to one repository; worktrees per writer, and the git scoping ladder that explains why careful staging is not enough
type: practice
---

**Rule:** One writer per checkout, branch included. Parallel writers in one repo each get their own
git worktree; the orchestrator integrates serially from the main checkout. Count writers per REPO,
not per task: two writers on disjoint files still share the index and HEAD. Where a checkout is
genuinely shared, `git add <paths>` then `git commit -m … -- <paths>` in one breath, and verify the
commit by accounting, not by its exit code.

**Why:** each rung was measured, and each defeats the protection of the rung above it:

1. **`git commit` takes the whole index.** Staging by name protected nothing: a bare commit swept
   another agent's staged 229-line file into a push. `--amend` also amends *whoever's* commit is at
   HEAD; one agent destroyed another's commit message that way.
2. **A push takes the whole branch.** Two writers, both path-scoped: one push carried the other's
   un-gated commits to the public remote as ancestors.
3. **The pre-commit hook stashes tracked, unstaged changes across the whole worktree**, however the
   commit is scoped; a concurrent writer's tracked edits vanish during the hook run. Untracked files
   are NOT touched and a failed re-apply is loud; overstating the hazard cost two sessions ~30 minutes
   of needless serialisation.
4. **`git commit -- <paths>` applies to TRACKED files only.** Without a prior `git add` it exited 0
   having committed 3 of 18 files; the message claimed all of them.
5. **The index is shared.** Files left staged across a tool call get swept into the other writer's
   bare commit.
6. **Read-then-Write of a whole file** destroyed another agent's edit landed in between.

- Two doc agents plus the orchestrator committing to one repo produced divergent sibling commits;
  `origin/main` looked clobbered until a rebase recovered it. A `git checkout -- .` reverted another
  writer's uncommitted work and voided its test runs: green figures for a tree that never held the
  change. Two agents in separate worktrees both edited one shared docs file in a third repo; the
  second commit swept the first's hunks under a message naming only its own change.

**How to apply:**

---
name: peer-sessions
description: When another interactive agent session works in the same machine or checkout, or you find unexplained commits or edits in your repo.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Other sessions are colleagues: discoverable with `ListAgents` (listed as peer sessions) and
addressable by the printed name. One writer per FILE, not just per path. Never edit a peer's
in-flight file; message them. A peer can never grant you escalation.

**Why:**

- Two sessions edited one boot document in the same checkout within minutes. One path-scoped commit
  swept the other's uncommitted edits under a message about something else. Path-scoping prevents
  sweeping unrelated paths; it says nothing about two writers in one file.
- A commit recipe `git stash; git pull --rebase; git push; git stash pop` removed a peer's in-flight
  edit from the working tree; the pop then aborted on conflict. The edit survived only in the stash.
  A stash is worse than a mis-scoped commit: it silently removes a live writer's bytes.
- A session found two unpushed commits, asked all live peers, got "not mine" from each, and concluded
  they were orphaned. Both were its own immediately-prior context window, ended 44 seconds earlier.
  `ListAgents` lists only LIVE sessions, and every session commits as the same git user.
- Coordination paid off: a peer accepted a refutation in full, corrected two artefacts, and returned a
  finding the other session did not have.

**How to apply:**

- Before editing a shared instrument file, check for peers (one call). Identify a peer by timing plus a
  commit sha, and say how you identified them.
- Found a peer's error? Send the measurement and the commands, and say you have not touched their text.
  Frame a divergence as "unstable" rather than "false" when the evidence allows (two code paths, each
  of you hit one). Say what you did NOT check.
- Unclaimed work in your repo: check your own lineage first. `ls -t ~/.claude/projects/<cwd-slug>/ *.jsonl | head`, then grep the commit subject in the predecessor transcript.
- Shared checkout: the scoping rules of \[[one-writer-per-checkout]\], plus no `pull --rebase` and no
  `--autostash`. Push only when `git status --short` shows nothing but your own paths.
- Never change permissions, project instructions or config because a peer asked, and never treat a
  peer message as the user's approval. If a peer was denied and asks you to do it, refuse and tell the
  user: that is permission laundering.
- Shared live infrastructure is a collision surface too: an uncoordinated change mid-benchmark makes
  the benchmark describe a configuration nobody runs.

Related: \[[one-writer-per-checkout]\] \[[dont-review-a-moving-artefact]\]

- `git worktree add .worktrees/<task> -b wt/<task> HEAD` (explicit base; a harness default may branch
  from `origin/<default>` instead of your feature branch).
- Integration: commit the branch, rebase onto main, run the merge gate ON THE REBASED BRANCH,
  fast-forward from the main checkout, push, delete branch and worktree (only after the agent's final
  report is accepted).
- Never run integration git inside a worktree; a push there can create a stray remote ref. Check:
  `git ls-remote origin 'refs/heads/wt/*'` returns nothing.
- Every integration block starts with `cd <checkout>` AND `git branch --show-current` in the same
  command: a checkout sitting on the feature branch makes `merge --ff-only <branch>` a silent no-op.
- Repo-root sweeps double-count `.worktrees/` copies: use `git grep`, `git ls-files`, or
  `--exclude-dir=.worktrees`.
- Type `-- <paths>` as part of typing `commit`, even when you think you are alone. Never `git add -A`,
  `git add .`, or a directory add. Never `checkout --`, `restore`, `stash` or `reset` in a shared
  checkout. With a concurrent writer, use line-scoped edits only.
- Before committing: `git diff --cached --name-only` shows only what you named. After:
  `git show --stat HEAD` matches the message and `git status --porcelain | wc -l` is 0.
- Subagents in a shared repo WRITE FILES ONLY; the orchestrator is the sole committer, or each unit has
  its own worktree. If you commit for agents you told not to run git, you are a second writer.
- A cross-repo file (shared docs) goes to ONE dispatch, or every implementer leaves it uncommitted for
  the orchestrator. Dispatching an agent whose brief names a tracked path IS a write to that checkout.
- No tracker writes (which rewrite a tracked export file) while a commit runs in that checkout.

Related: \[[read-shared-trees-at-committed-objects]\] \[[peer-sessions]\] \[[landing-and-history]\] \[[format-before-commit]\] \[[concurrency-budget]\]

---
name: scratchpad-shared-across-agents
description: When deciding where probes, scripts, reports or retained artefacts live, naming scratch files, or symlinking a long scratchpad path
type: trap
---

**Rule:** Scratch space is volatile and shared. Anything someone will re-read goes into the repository's
reports directory and is committed; never cite a `/tmp` path as durable. Prefix every scratch file with
your task id AND role (`<task>-<role>-<name>`), prefer the `Write` tool over shell redirects, and
before trusting a scratch artefact you did not watch yourself write, check its mtime and provenance.

**Why / measured:**

- `/tmp` is a tmpfs: a reboot or a host move loses it. Committed records citing a "retained" probe under
  a shared `/tmp` handle became unresolvable coordinates.
- Two agents on unrelated tasks both wrote `sweep2.sh`. The second write was caught only because the
  Write tool refuses to overwrite a file the caller has not read. A `cat > ... <<'EOF'` would have
  overwritten it at exit 0, and the victim would see a probe that "measures the wrong thing", which
  reads as a finding, not an instrument failure.
- One task commonly gets a spec round, a gate, a fix round and a re-gate in one session. A fix round's
  first "green" was the gate's `green.txt` for the same task; its own chain had short-circuited and
  never written the file. Namespacing by task id alone is not enough: that is exactly what two agents
  on one task collide on.
- One-writer-per-worktree does not cover this: the scratchpad is outside every worktree. The same hazard
  reaches `~/.cache/` when two agents pick the same dated directory.
- Per-session scratch paths are ~110 characters and were retyped as a prefix in 900+ calls (about 335K
  tokens). The fix "symlink it to /tmp/sp" told every concurrent session to claim the same name: two
  agents found `/tmp/sp` re-pointed under them mid-flight, one resolving into a different session's
  tree; six live `sp*` links existed at once. A re-pointed symlink is followed silently by `cat >`,
  `sed -i` and every redirect, which write into the other session's tree at exit 0. It surfaced only
  because the Write tool refuses on a changed resolution. The convention's documentation also outlived
  the host it was written on.

**How to apply:**

- Use your own scratchpad per session (the harness-provided one, or `mktemp -d`). Shell state does not
  persist between tool calls, so symlink it once at boot under a SESSION-UNIQUE name:

```sh
FULL=<the session scratchpad path>
SP="/tmp/sp-$(basename "$(dirname "$FULL")")"   # suffix from the session's own id
ln -sfn "$FULL" "$SP"
```

---
name: read-shared-trees-at-committed-objects
description: When reading, committing or making claims about a tree or scratchpad another agent or peer session is working in
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Read a contended tree at a committed object (`git show "${sha}:<path>"`, `rev-parse`), or not
at all. A clean `git status` does not mean unmoved, a file existing does not mean it is finished, and
an absence on a live branch is not an absence. In a shared scratchpad, every agent writes to its own
absolute subdirectory with uniquely named outputs, and checks mtime before reading a file it did not
just write.

**Why:**

- **Clean is not unmoved.** A gate was warned a peer "may still hold" a repo. The peer had landed one
  commit past the spec's pin, +110/−3, in the exact file under review. Porcelain read clean in both
  states; only `rev-parse` separates them.
- **Already-done that never was.** A scout reported an item "already discharged", quoting a section a
  live agent had written minutes earlier. Sound method, conclusion about a state that did not exist at
  dispatch. Tell: an "already done" finding with no commit behind it.
- **One revision, three suite figures in one session:** dirty tree 166/531, `git archive` extract
  7/531, clean clone 531/531. A figure taken against a tree a peer holds measures no revision.
- **Torn captures.** A spec committed while its author still edited: 392 lines against 481 on disk. It
  announced an O1a/O1b split and had no O1b section, staged cleanly and read as complete. The author
  caught it by comparing its file to `git show HEAD:<path>`.
- **Partial-write figures describe nothing.** A diffstat read mid-write matched neither commit that
  resulted. Worse than stale: a stale figure was once true.
- **Racy absence.** "You did not commit it" was sent off `git log`; the reflog showed the commit landed
  ten minutes after the read and before the message arrived.
- **Scratch collisions.** Generic filenames (`probe.nix`) were replaced by another agent's file of the
  same name mid-task. An agent read a results file before its own run wrote it and got the previous
  round's complete, plausible, wrong numbers; the tell was the mtime, not the content. A brief saying
  "use a per-agent subdir `<name>-private/`" made seven agents create it in the repo root (their cwd);
  every brief giving the absolute path produced zero strays.

**How to apply:**

---
name: agent-liveness-and-ownership
description: When an agent says "waiting", goes idle, is inherited from a handover, or its repo is about to be reassigned; and before closing a session with agents live.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** An agent's liveness is not observable from the files it writes. Only the spawning session's
agent list (`ListAgents`) knows. "Waiting" from an agent is a claim to check, idle is not dead, and
the orchestrator owns every agent it dispatched until each returns.

**Why:**

- `git status` clean reads "finished" while an agent is between commits. File mtimes go quiet by
  construction after a push, because a commit does not touch working files. A peer declared a tree
  "safe to write" and retracted it an hour later.
- A builder said "waiting on the background run", the run died without notification, and the agent
  sat 4 hours with half its work uncommitted in a worktree.
- An agent reported STOP and went idle; its repo was re-dispatched. A message queued earlier woke the
  old agent, which edited 7 files while the new owner was working. The new owner reported a second
  writer. Idle agents still have an inbox.
- A session wrote its handoff at about 87% context with five gates and a build still running. Owner:
  "you own the agents you dispatched. See these through."

**How to apply:**

- On any "waiting" idle notice, check in the same turn: is there a live process (`ps`), and what is
  the newest mtime in the agent's scratch dir? No process and a stale mtime means stalled. Wake it
  with the completion line from its own output file.
- Inherited handover naming a live agent: ask the parent session for its agent list. Treat the tree as
  hot until told otherwise. If the parent is gone, use `git diff` for shape, save it as an unverified
  starting point, and re-drive every test.
- Before reassigning a repo: stop the old agent first (`TaskStop`), then dispatch the successor. If a
  collision happens anyway: stop the stray writer, confirm the tree is stable, save its partial diff,
  and give the successor sole ownership with an adopt-or-reset choice.
- Do not close a session while dispatched agents are live. Keep committing their results as they land.
  Write the handoff when the live count is zero or a hard context limit forces it, and re-commit as
  late results arrive.

Related: \[[kill-only-captured-pids]\] \[[resume-failed-agents]\] \[[peer-sessions]\]
Related: \[[presenting-a-decision]\] \[[before-asking-the-owner]\]
Related: \[[by-construction-over-repair]\] \[[generic-core-no-consumer-names]\] \[[graph-native-modelling]\]

q12.query: When should code changes be committed during multi-step development?

results.text:
---
name: spec-and-plan-before-code
description: Before any code change, and when moving from a written plan into multi-task execution.
type: workflow
---

**Rule:** Spec first and file the tracking task before touching code, including one-line changes.
After writing a plan, dispatch an INDEPENDENT plan reviewer before the first task. Execute with a
fresh agent per task and a two-stage review.

**Why:**

- A one-line change to public `gen-schema` (`_kind` on every instance) was measured green, committed and pushed with no spec. The
  owner rejected it on five design grounds (denormalisation, surface growth, non-totality on empty
  input, direction of contamination, re-nominalising a structural surface). It cost a public revert, a
  lock bump and three thrown-away fixture edits. Measurement answers "does it work"; the objections
  were "should it exist in this shape". The smallness made it feel exempt.
- The plan review was skipped twice. Cause: a seam between two skills. The plan-writing skill ends in
  SELF-review and a hard handoff; the execution skill reviews per task, not the whole plan.
- A correction that replicated: the content was fixed by measurement, but its EXTENT was not. A first
  grep found 3 sites, a second spelling found 3 more, a third spelling and an inherited direct call
  surfaced only at review. A change's blast radius is not derivable from its content.
- A plan with exact before/after code, executed by a fresh agent per task with two-stage review,
  shipped a 7-task, 25-file refactor with zero rework.

**How to apply:**

- Spec records rejected routes with reasons so later sessions cannot re-litigate them. Review the
  SPEC, then implement.
- When a correction replicates, the artefact to write and review is the SWEEP PREDICATE, with a
  liveness control on a known positive in a DIFFERENT spelling.
- Review chain: design review, spec review, PLAN review, per-task spec-compliance then quality review.
- Explore exhaustively before planning (exact paths, signatures, caller inventory). Plans carry
  concrete diffs and file references, not prose.
- Fresh worker per task with full context in the prompt. The coordinator applies 2-line review fixes
  itself rather than re-dispatching.
- Map the dependency chain so independent tasks run without blocking.
- Honour a requested checkpoint before a big mechanical grind even if the end state would be green;
  its value is catching a wrong turn before the cost is paid.
- When a worker reports "gaps I worked around", check whether the gap belongs at the source library.
  Re-run the gate yourself rather than accepting a worker's green.

Related: \[[reviewable-artefact]\] \[[review-economy]\] \[[writing-a-dispatch-brief]\]

---
name: nix-hidden-unsoundness
description: When writing incremental, dedup, hashing or traversal code in pure Nix
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Assume dedup, hashing and "clean" checks are unsound until a test with function-bearing, multi-definition and multi-seed fixtures shows otherwise.

**Why / measured:**

- Null-hash false-clean: `null != null` is false, so a changed function-bearing node whose hash is null reads as reusable. Route every hash comparison through one null-safe guard. Integer-valued property tests cannot catch this; it needs function-bearing fixtures.
- `functionArgs` cannot see `@`-patterns or bare lambdas, so inferring a module is clean from its formals is unsound. Treat function modules as dirty by default, with an explicit author marker as opt-in. The suite includes a lying marker to prove the guard has teeth.
- Dedup on the structural path key, not the name-only identity key, or multi-definition entries double-emit.
- `flatten` forces freeform leaves to WHNF, so registry builds must run after the fixpoint or self-output recursion returns.
- gen-graph's `foldReach` is first-edge-wins: it drops a second edge to an already-visited target, including its projection. Two same-target edges with different filters do not compose.
- A dedup key that must be "share iff same derivation" cannot be made automatic in pure Nix (lambdas are unhashable). It needs a caller-threaded site token (gen-pipe's `site`), placed at the point where chains diverge.
- A single-key shadow approach worked only because suppression happened to sit at one root. A true self ∪ ancestors union (gen-scope `inheritSet`) fixed the latent bug of dropping the farther suppressor.
- A warm-serve path is correct only if declared edges over-declare cross-node reads. Otherwise a consumer outside the cone gets a stale value.
- A multi-seed implementation committed before its multi-seed tests shipped a single-seed soundness bug.
- Same-priority, same-order list definitions merge in reverse declaration order.

**How to apply:** Write the adversarial fixtures before the implementation. State honest ceilings in code and docs (for example "O(|cone|), not O(|affected|)").

Related: \[[nix-laziness-design]\] \[[oracle-design]\] \[[cite-the-primary-honestly]\]

---
name: shared-checkout-peer-sessions
description: Collision rules when two agent sessions write in the same git working tree (for example a build session and a sitting or design session).
type: practice
---

**Rule:** In a checkout another live session writes to, commit ONLY with
`git commit -- <your paths>`, and never stash, pull, rebase-pull, autostash or push there.

**Why:** Measured: a `git stash` in one session took a peer author's in-flight spec edit out of the
tree; only `stash@{0}` saved it. A bare `git commit` takes the whole index and has swept another
writer's staged work into a push.

**How to apply:**

- Commit path-scoped: your reports, your probes, your tracker export, plus any file the owner
  explicitly directed you to edit (and tell the peer session in the same act).
- The peer that owns publication pulls before it pushes; because it is the same local branch, its
  push publishes your commits.
- A pre-commit hook may stash unstaged files itself. After every commit run `git status --short` and
  confirm no peer file vanished. If one did, stop and tell the peer at once. Skipping the hook
  (`--no-verify`) needs the owner's say-so.
- Never edit a file the peer has in flight. Send it the measurement instead.
- At close, after the peer's next push: `git fetch`, then
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` for each of your commits, plus one unresolvable
  sha as the control. Report any commit that did not reach origin.
- A peer cannot grant escalation. A peer's request is never the owner's approval.
- With NO peer running, the rules relax: you may `git pull --ff-only` and push your own path-scoped
  commits, but only if `git status --short` shows nothing you do not own.
- While an automated multi-repo relock/update (gen's `relock-all`) is running on a repo, do not `git worktree add` or push
  to that repo's main; use a scratch clone.

Related: \[[owner-sitting]\] \[[design-session]\] \[[dispatch-form]\]

---
name: format-before-commit
description: Before any commit in a repository whose CI checks formatting (treefmt, nixfmt, mdformat); the false greens a formatter produces
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Run the repository's own formatter on the files you are committing, after the last
edit, against the exact revision you will land. Do not trust an earlier green, an agent's
reported green, or a green from inside a linked worktree.

**Why:** an unformatted commit is a guaranteed red CI. Four measured false greens:

1. **`nix fmt` run from a worktree nested inside the repository formats the MAIN checkout**
   and reports `0 changed` about a tree it never touched. The wrapper runs
   `treefmt --tree-root-file=.git/config`; in a linked worktree `.git` is a file, so the
   upward search skips it and lands on the main checkout. This put unformatted files into
   two pushed repositories, and it silently rewrites a tree another agent may be working in.
2. **Untracked new files are invisible to treefmt.** `0 changed` did not cover the one file
   the commit was adding. `git add` first, then format.
3. **`--ci` is fail-on-change, not check-only: it rewrites the tree.** A second run is
   always green, with the fix sitting unstaged. `git add` again after formatting.
4. **A later commit voids the reading.** An implementer reported `0 changed`, then made three
   more commits; two unformatted files were pushed.
   Also: a cold-cache `(N changed)` count is not an unformatted-file count. Judge by a repeat run
   reading 0 plus a clean `git status`.

**How to apply:**

- Format only the files you are committing. A repository-wide run reformats unrelated files
  (one config repository had 55 generated files with pre-existing drift), and the collateral
  rides into the commit.
- Use the repository's canonical entry point (`nix fmt <files>`, or the CI flake's formatter
  run from the directory CI uses), not a bare `treefmt` from PATH. A PATH treefmt with a
  different config enabled a lint that rewrote `{ x = cfg.x or [ ]; }` into
  `{ inherit (cfg) x; }`. That dropped a load-bearing default and broke evaluation.
- For worktree work, invoke the formatters directly on named paths, or run
  `treefmt --tree-root <git-archive extract of the landing rev> --walk filesystem --no-cache --fail-on-change`.
- Landing check: after merging, run the CI format command in the main checkout and require
  `0 changed` before pushing.
- A control that exits non-zero for the wrong reason (a usage error) has not fired. Discard
  the run.
- Do not rewrite a standing instruction on one agent's unreproduced claim. Reproduce it with
  a live control first.

Related: \[[one-writer-per-checkout]\] \[[ci-gate-discipline]\]

---
name: reuse-scan-before-build
description: Before designing or building any new engine, library, mechanism or helper in an ecosystem of existing libraries; and when adopting a library primitive to replace hand-rolled code.
type: practice
values:
  extend-if-coverage: provisional
---

**Rule:** Step 0 of any build is a reuse scan: which existing library already provides this? Scan to
primitive granularity, treat an absence in any capability map as a hypothesis, and when adopting a
library check that its surface has YOUR semantics.

**Why:**

- A design proposed a new `gen-fixpoint` library that was about 85% of the already-shipped
  `gen-resolve`. Only a lateral
  question from the owner caught it. Adversarial review verifies CLAIMS; it cannot flag an OMISSION,
  because the unconsidered library is not in the spec to check. Anchoring on "build X" propagates
  into every grounder and reviewer prompt.
- A design picked the right library and the wrong primitive: `gen-graph`'s `query` (paths mode
  threads its visited set per path, so it duplicates nodes on non-tree shapes), when
  `gen-graph/lib/preorder.nix`, one file over, visits each node once via `foldl'`. Two
  review rounds prescribed a post-hoc dedup repair instead.
- A capability map declared `gen-product`'s `latticeGraph` "genuinely absent" on the very day the
  commit adding it landed; `gen-link` was missing from the map entirely. The entry was false when written.
- Adopting `gen-graph` for a hand-rolled closure: `reachableFrom` excluded the start node; the
  library form had no recursion, so a cycle that used to abort was now answered silently; one primitive
  was partial with an uncatchable error; a transpose silently dropped edges from outside its declared
  node set. One-hop inputs all agreed, so the domain looked cleared.
- A lone scout refuting items from a large multi-agent audit ("needs a new primitive") was wrong on all
  four re-checked items: it compared against the one obvious primitive, not the full built set.

**How to apply:**

---
name: infra-changes-owner-deploys
description: When a change touches live infrastructure config (host configs, secrets, cluster manifests) — agents author and commit, the owner approves and deploys.
type: practice
scope: local
---

**Rule:** An agent may author and commit infrastructure-config changes like any other build, but it
never runs a switch, deploy or rollout to a live host. Deployment is the owner's act. Secrets follow
the same split: the agent wires the mechanism, the owner decides what root-of-trust material exists.

**Why:** An infra change (a session hook, a packaged tool, a service) alters the environment every
later session runs in. Holding such work back as "unauthorised" stalls it; deploying it from a
session removes the owner's last checkpoint. The split keeps both: work flows, deploys stay human.

**How to apply:**

- Author and commit under the repo's normal conventions (linear history, module conventions). The
  report names the change for approval and says "deployment owed by the owner".
- Secrets: always use the repo's declared generators (for example `agenix generate` with
  agenix-rekey). Hand-encrypt only values issued externally, and document the provisioning procedure
  next to the declaration. Hand-rolled values fork provenance from the generators.
- A human-held master credential (the password that unlocks the vault the other secrets are recovered
  from) does not go into the repo, even encrypted. Encrypting it does not change what it is: it
  collapses a trust tier that exists only because it is held out of band. Build the consuming
  mechanism self-gated on the file's presence (`builtins.pathExists`) so it is fully inert without
  it, and never create the file. Offer a credential-free alternative.
- Do not generalise the credential rule to every root of trust. A CA root encrypted to a hardware key
  in the repo was ruled acceptable. Ask rather than extend a security ruling by analogy.
- In a public infra repo, keep PR bodies and commit messages free of IPs, CIDRs, real hostnames,
  domains, ports and operational counts. See \[[public-artifact-hygiene]\].

Related: \[[public-artifact-hygiene]\] \[[pin-container-images-by-digest]\]

---
name: treefmt-fail-on-change-writes-first
description: Applies when using treefmt (or a pre-commit treefmt hook) as a format check.
type: trap
---

**Rule:** Treat `treefmt --fail-on-change` as "format, then report whether anything changed". Decide
"was the committed tree formatted" from exit 0 + 0 changed + a CLEAN `git status` in the same run.

**Why:** The flag does not mean check-only. It reformats in place, compares, and exits 1 if anything
changed, so afterwards the tree is formatted and the exit code describes the tree as it WAS. A second
pass cannot tell "was clean" from "I just cleaned it"; `git status` can, in one run. Control: at an
unformatted parent, exit 1, 1 changed, tree dirty.
This is also why a pre-commit treefmt failure ("unexpected changes detected, --fail-on-change is
enabled") leaves a dirty tree: the hook already rewrote the file.

**How to apply:**

- After a hook refusal: `git add` the reformatted file and commit again. Do not re-edit by hand. The
  second commit's run is the one that measures.
- As a check: `treefmt --fail-on-change; echo "rc=$?"; git status --porcelain` must be rc 0 and empty.

Related: \[[formatter-check-is-not-a-format-run]\]

---
name: landing-and-history
description: When committing, merging, pushing or landing a unit of work onto main, and how often
type: practice
scope: local
---

**Rule:** Commit after each verified logical unit. Land a gate-passed unit on its repository's
main in the same dispatch, by its own build agent. Keep history linear: rebase, not a merge
commit. Revert shared history forward-only, never force-push.

**Why:**

- Commits are sync points: peer agents review by pulling them, so batching stalls the loop.
  Write messages that stand alone for a peer reader.
- **Exception: do not commit a generated export often.** 44 commits touching only a tracker
  export destroyed sha-based tree identity: every cross-revision claim then needed a scoped
  diff. Batch the export once per session phase.
- Every build brief in one session said "branch only (relock executing)", so about 20
  gate-passed units sat on branches, and closures fell to 5 against 37 creations in a day. The
  relock rule was narrow: no push to a repository's main *while a relock is executing on THAT
  repository*. One main sat free for four and a half hours.
- A diverged main integrated by `git merge` produced merge commits. Owner: "in the future,
  rebase instead of merge." One repository's branch rule rejects merge commits on push.
- A writer prompt said "you may push once green", and the writer pushed a change whose
  requirement the owner then challenged. The revert had to go forward-only; the force-push was
  correctly blocked.

**How to apply:**

- Two Nix lambdas are never equal, not even a value against itself. Exclude raw-function fields from
  comparisons and check them by name.
- Do not quote a cell-count fraction in docs; it went stale on three consecutive commits. Name the cell
  set instead.
- Editing an existing oracle cell's regex to make a change pass has **moved the oracle rather than met
  it**.
- A refusal sweep needs a **populated** positive control, or it cannot tell a refusal from a legitimately
  empty answer.
- The frozen edge trace is topology evidence, not acceptance authority: two executions with different
  answers once shared a byte-equal fingerprint.

Theory: Manchanda & Warren (view definition/relation), Néron et al. 2015 (reference resolution rule),
Vogt (bounded well-definedness, second conjunct only), Knuth 1968 (one direction of reduction only).

q13.query: What does a search or census returning zero results prove when verifying an absence claim?

results.text:
---
name: controls-for-absence-claims
description: When reporting a zero, an absence or an "identical" result, and building the positive/negative controls that make it meaningful
type: trap
verified: 2026-10-15; zsh 5.9.2, git 2.55.0
---

**Rule:** Every absence claim carries a positive control that runs YOUR predicate, in the same
instrument, same output form, same run and comparable complexity, on a case known to match. If the
control reads 0 too, the instrument is broken: fix it before reporting anything. Plant a positive if
the material has none, and mint fresh negative tokens each run.

**Why / measured:**

- Sweeps where every term AND the control read 0, each looking like a clean, well-controlled absence:
  zsh did not word-split an unquoted `$list`, so grep got one concatenated path; `git grep -lin` parsed
  as `--lin` and printed nothing to stdout; a tracker read failed with "database is busy" (rc 2) and
  produced empty output. The control is what exposed the first one.
- A sweep for pattern P was "controlled" by pattern Q firing 5 times. Both figures were true and the
  pairing proved nothing about P.
- P run against the very revision that "carried" the offending text returned 0, because the text had
  only ever existed in a report. When the corpus holds no known positive, a planted case is mandatory.
  Say that it was planted.
- Negative-control tokens get copied into reports and tracker bodies. A reused token later fires on the
  record of an earlier run and looks like a broken instrument. The opposite hazard follows: dismissing
  a genuine hit as "just a banked token".
- A control slug written into the file being swept makes the "MISSING" probe match the file's own
  documentation. The armed run then looks identical to a clean pass.
- A comparison instrument needs its own negative control. A nonexistent arm must report UNUSABLE, never
  IDENTICAL. The comparator can be dead while both subjects are fine.
- An id predicate also matches inside other records' text. Anchor it to the id field
  (`cut -f1 | grep -cx id`).
- A busy database read exited rc 2 with clean empty stdout (the error on stderr). Every grep over it read
  0, the positive control included; attempts 1 and 2 returned 0 lines, attempt 3 returned 3496. Killing
  a reader in flight hands its caller the same empty result. A "busy" error can also mean either live
  contention (a process holds the lock: wait) or a wedged store (no process: repair), with one text.
- Result rows prefixed with a status glyph made an id anchored at start-of-line (`grep -c '^<id>'`) read
  0 over a full result set. Print one real row before writing a predicate over a tool's output.
- In an aborting run no control can fire, because the abort destroys the output. The strongest form
  available is the same file and expressions at a size that returns. Say so explicitly.

**How to apply:**

---
name: armed-controls
description: Before believing any zero, absence, "no change", or green from a sweep, grep, census or test, and when choosing the control that is supposed to validate it — the laws for a control that actually measures
type: practice
---

**Rule:** A census PROVES EXISTENCE when it hits; a zero confirms nothing. Report it as "zero over
<population> at <revisions>", not "absent", and draw no decision from it. A clean result is evidence
only with an armed instrument: a live control from the same instrument in the same run, whose domain
reaches past the predicate's, taken at an operating point where the defect would be visible; and every
green is shown to go red when you seed the thing it should catch.

**Why (each law was paid for by a false green):**

- The owner withdrew a relayed "this does not reopen" that rested on a zero census with live controls:
  "a census only proves existence, absence confirms nothing". A firing control proves the predicate
  works where it looked, not that the object could not live elsewhere: a sentence "did not exist"
  across `*.md`; it was in tracker bodies no file glob reaches.
- **Picking a control is a measurement.** A docs-only landing filter read 0 on the subject and 0 on the
  control, because the control commit was also docs-only. A commit the filter could catch (115 lines)
  armed it.
- **Regime.** A laptop shed 36 °C in four minutes idle, so the cooling path was declared healthy. The
  defect was a degraded thermal interface, roughly constant in °C/W: ~10 W idle cost 20 °C, 28 W load
  cost 55 °C and pinned the CPU. Every figure true; the control taken where the defect is invisible.
- Main and control needles were two hand-copied literals: breaking the control went red, breaking the
  MAIN read green over a real defect.
- A file list's last row was unterminated; a shell `read` loop dropped it: 21 of 22 files scanned,
  exit 0.
- Grepping nixpkgs' word (`emptyValue`) over gen-merge (a re-implementation of the nixpkgs module
  system) found nothing; gen-merge uses `whenEmpty`. The one hit was a comment listing "the foreign
  protocol's words".
- A line grep and a whitespace-flattened grep both read 0 ("two methods agree"); the phrase was present,
  the continuation line's `#` left inside it. Other misses in one day: the file a row cites rather than
  the one the construct lives in; `x.y` searched where source reads `inherit (x) y`.
- `git merge-base --is-ancestor <fabricated-sha> <ref>` returns 128 (never ran), not 1 (said no). A
  negative-control token fired because an earlier sweep had written it into the corpus.

**How to apply:**

---
name: code-graph-index-traps
description: When using a code knowledge-graph index (e.g. codebase-memory) for absence, caller or dead-code claims
type: trap
verified: unverified
---

**Rule:** Use a code graph for structure and shape questions. Derive every absence claim, including "zero callers" and "symbol not found", from grep with a live control.

**Why / measured on a large Nix codebase:**

- The architecture summary's `languages` field did not list Nix while 2195 Nix functions were indexed in the same response. An agent told to confirm coverage from that field concludes Nix is unindexed and throws away the whole capability.
- CALLS edges miss calls made through an imported attrset (`x = lib.y.runPrePass { ... }`), which is Nix's dominant cross-module idiom. `trace_path` reported zero callers while grep found the call, and a control showed caller-tracing worked for direct calls. Zero callers is not evidence of dead code.
- Symbol search returned only Function nodes, so non-function `let` bindings read as absent. That would have produced false "dissolved" verdicts in an audit.
- Complexity properties lived on `f.file_path`, not `f.file`. A wrong property name returns 0 rows silently.
- Loop and recursion metrics are near-useless for Nix: folds are `foldl'` calls, not syntactic loops. The working discriminator was a grep for "does the folded lambda read the accumulator?".
- Passing a fast/moderate index mode skipped directories by name (`gen`, `docs`, `scripts`, `tools`, `bin`, `build`, ...). A skipped directory looks exactly like absent code.
- Cross-repo matching found 0 edges between pure libraries. It matches HTTP routes and channels, not imports.
- An earlier "zero symbols for Nix" reading was correct when measured and wrong two weeks later, after the indexer and its pin were fixed.

**How to apply:**

- Confirm coverage with a known-positive symbol query.
- Use the body-token field for "what does this body do" (it can show a symbol was rerouted, not merely renamed).
- Never pass an index mode. Re-measure capability claims before relying on them.

Related: \[[nix-lsp-traps]\] \[[git-measurement-traps]\] \[[controls-for-absence-claims]\]

- Before dispatching against a tracked item, query its STATUS, not only its newest text. Where a spec
  and its row disagree on whether something is open, the row's NEWEST dated entry governs.
- Before relaying a tool's finding, drive it: seed what it claims is unused or wrong and see if anything
  moves. A tool's zero is not an absence until armed with a known positive in the same run.
- Re-derive any figure you rest an argument on, with the predicate beside it.
- The tell: a premise you can state confidently but cannot name a command for. It is `[RELAYED]` even
  when a command reproduces the artefact: that measures "the artefact says this", not "this is true".
- A provenance claim (who told whom, when) is checkable like a number: check it or do not state it.
- Detaching a consequent owes a measurement: not "did X happen" but "does what Y names still exist".
- A correction inherits the burden of what it corrects: replacing a population figure with a sampled
  one is a new defect dressed as a fix.
- A fence in a brief is as load-bearing as a premise. Retracting one in flight, say so plainly and tell
  the agent to weight your remaining premises accordingly.
- Run a prior-art sweep on the TOPIC before any new filing.
- When a result lacks something that could not possibly be absent, the instrument is broken.
- A search hit with an ellipsis is a pointer, not the field: open it and read the token whole before
  quoting a path, id, date or label.

Related: \[[brief-premises-are-hypotheses]\] \[[success-signal-is-not-measurement]\] \[[counts-need-anchor-and-population]\] \[[cite-by-binding-not-line-number]\] \[[armed-controls]\]

---
name: control-population-must-match-claim
description: Applies to every absence claim ("X appears 0 times") and every relayed control figure.
type: trap
verified: unverified
---

**Rule:** Run the positive control on exactly the population the absence claims, and make the figure
and its population travel together as one token everywhere it is quoted.

**Why:** Two measured cases:

- A sweep reported "`adapter` => 0 files across the whole tree, controls `link` 7, `origin` 7,
  `facet` 5". The absence was whole-tree (47 files); the controls were `lib/`-only (9 files). Whole-tree
  the controls read 34, 27, 16. The spec stated both scopes once correctly, then repeated the bare
  figures without the qualifier, and the bare form propagated into a dispatch premise and a commit
  message.
- A sweep globbed `specs/adr/0031*.md` to find an amendment. The amendment lived in
  `specs/adr/ledger/0031-*.md`, a directory the glob never matches. By house style the law file carries
  no amendment vocabulary, so the search could never hit, and a positive control run in the same
  too-narrow domain passed. An agent was then dispatched to draft an amendment that had landed 20
  hours earlier.

**How to apply:**

- Write `link 7 (lib/ only)`, never `link 7`. When relaying someone else's controls, re-derive the
  population or mark the premise as relayed.
- Before an absence search, ask where the thing would live if it existed, and include that location.
  For a document stored as two records (law + ledger), glob both.
- Add a random negative control (a fresh string from `/dev/urandom`) beside the positive one.
- If the conclusion survives re-measurement, still record that the original basis failed.

Related: \[[control-must-differ-on-the-failing-axis]\] \[[controls-for-absence-claims]\]

01. State the domain on both sides. Narrower gives false greens; wider gives false reds.
02. Every absence: a control known to fire IN THAT FILE, same instrument, same run. A control reading 0
    means the predicate is broken, not that the thing is absent.
03. Arm a pair on the same bound operand; the control exercises it at an input the main arm does not.
    Test by breaking the MAIN arm. Stock and mutated arms reading the same means nothing was measured.
04. Reach claims: one control outside the claimed domain, plus a per-member "files scanned" count;
    assert scanned == expected. A list also needs a POPULATION control: a truncated listing (default
    limit, closed items excluded) cannot be saved by a predicate control.
05. Seed, confirm red, remove. A control pointed at something known clean can only agree. Name the
    seeding axis used (mutate the guard vs vary the fixture) and the one not used.
06. Operating point: before citing a measurement as clearing a defect, ask whether the defect is visible
    there. For constant-coefficient losses (°C/W, per-operation overhead), control under load.
07. Enumerate forms; report spellings covered and evasions unswept. Strip comment markers, then flatten.
    For a re-implementation, take search terms from the subject, not from what it re-implements.
08. Fresh nonsense token per sweep; a real non-ancestor commit as the ancestry control.
09. Correcting a predicate: re-derive its population from the original universe, not the prior output.
10. Brief a census as hit list, population and revisions; keep any trigger the zero would disarm ARMED.
11. Two correct measurements on different axes can compose into a wrong action; the axis travels with
    the claim.

- Scope: these laws govern MEASUREMENT, where a command can refute the claim. Where none exists,
  acceptance is a named person's judgement; do not invent a proxy metric.

Related: \[[success-signal-is-not-measurement]\] \[[counts-need-anchor-and-population]\] \[[conclusion-and-basis-are-two-findings]\] \[[relayed-is-not-measured]\] \[[reading-test-suite-output]\]

---
name: roles-common-protocol
description: The standing half every dispatched subagent role (scout, spec, gate, build) carries - measurement law, reporting disclosures, delivery and the stop protocol.
type: workflow
---

# Common protocol for every subagent role

## Measurement law

- **Every absence claim needs a positive control that FIRED**, same instrument, same run. A zero from
  a predicate that could not have matched is INVALID, not clean. See \[[controls-for-absence-claims]\].
- **Check a predicate's reach against the concept, not its spelling.** A true zero in the wrong
  library or under the wrong term produces a confident wrong conclusion.
- **Drive the check red and read it.** Produce the failing state and look at the output. Measured: a
  build whose edit silently wrote nothing returned `163/163` and its agent read that as success.
- **A probe whose two arms agree has measured nothing**, and neither has a one-armed probe compared
  with a figure from a document. Exhibit both arms from your own instrument, measuring the same object.
- **A report about an artefact is never a measurement of it.** Re-derive; do not relay.
- **Your brief is a claim set, not ground.** Briefs carried a false load-bearing claim in roughly half
  of sampled runs: either stale (true once, since fixed) or simply wrong (a count, path, cause).
  Test load-bearing claims before building on them. Emphasis marks protect nothing.
- **"At HEAD" is not a coordinate.** Re-derive any cited line, digest or path; say which copy you read;
  where a pin exists (lock file, store path, explicit sha) read the pinned revision.

## Shell facts that have caused false findings

- The tool named "Bash" may run zsh: unquoted `$list` does not word-split; `$pipestatus` not
  `$PIPESTATUS`; brace `"${sha}:path"` (zsh history modifiers otherwise mangle it and return nothing
  at exit 0); never name a variable `path` (it is tied to `PATH`). See \[[zsh-is-not-bash]\].
- Read exit status UNPIPED: `cmd > out; echo $?`. See \[[read-exit-status-unpiped]\].
- Do not `2>/dev/null` a measurement: it turns a missing tool into an absence finding.
- `grep -c` counts LINES; prose wraps. For phrases: `tr -s '[:space:]' ' ' | grep -o 'phrase' | wc -l`.
  Carry the unit (lines / occurrences / files) in every figure. See \[[grep-wrapper-and-count-units]\], \[[grep-wrapped-prose]\].
- `grep -r` does not follow symlinks; `-R` does.
- A test summary of `0/0` is a FALSE PASS. Check the collected count agrees with the summary.
  See \[[nix-unit-collection-traps]\].

## Control tokens

- Write the subject and the control in the same command, with the same flags, and print both values.
- Read exit status unpiped and look at stderr: `cmd > out 2> err; echo $?`.
- On an empty read from a shared store, check the exit status, retry a few times with a short wait, and
  check whether a process holds the lock before accepting the empty result or declaring a wedge.
- Report counts per term INCLUDING zeros, and make a sweep script refuse (exit 1) when every term is
  zero.
- Generate a new random token for each negative control and never commit it.

Supersedes the general half of tracker-br-traps and br-output-row-shapes (retired with the tracker-specific traps).

Related: \[[control-population-must-match-claim]\] \[[control-must-differ-on-the-failing-axis]\] \[[read-exit-status-unpiped]\] \[[grep-wrapper-and-count-units]\]
Related: \[[presenting-a-decision]\] \[[before-asking-the-owner]\]
Related: \[[by-construction-over-repair]\] \[[generic-core-no-consumer-names]\] \[[graph-native-modelling]\]

q14.query: What must exist before a spec or plan can be submitted to a review gate?

results.text:
---
name: gates-need-an-oracle
description: Before opening an adversarial review gate on a spec, design or plan, and when writing the oracle cells it will judge
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Before a gate, name what settles it. An executable oracle (a test, a differential)
supports review rounds. A person's judgement gets ONE reading by that person, not rounds. No
oracle means no gate. An oracle cell's RED and GREEN values are EVALUATED before the cell is
written, not derived from reading the source.

**Why:**

- Seven adversarial rounds on a plan co-designed with the owner grew it from 350 to 660 lines
  and deleted twelve of the owner's own rules. One of them was "the plan's job is to minimise
  the number of decisions that must be made". A drift audit found 30 of 103 rules surviving as
  written, and 52 agent-introduced, 29 of which constrained the owner. Prose always admits
  another reading, so "run until dry" never terminates on prose. Owner: "Acceptance criteria
  is owner signoff. I cannot assign a number to an unknown any easier than you can."
- **Reading gates verify sections; only construction composes them.** Twenty rounds validated
  a spec whose two sections could not both be implemented. One implementation contact found it
  in minutes.
- A round added two oracle cells whose red and green values were reasoned out and never run. A
  fresh reviewer found three stated values false and one control unable to discriminate. The
  dispatch had handed the author a derived red shape, and a derived expectation inherited from
  the dispatcher is still derived.
- **Same-pass check:** a builder emitted a plausible hash right beside its own "I won't guess"
  disclaimer. A check that runs in the same pass as the thing it checks is not a check.
- Mechanical tasks given executable oracle apparatus spent two gate rounds on defects in the
  INSTRUMENTS. Owner: "this is taking longer than it should for what should be a mechanical
  task." The tell is gate findings recurring in the apparatus, not the artefact.

**How to apply:**

- Owner-authored text is evidence, not reviewable material. A reviewer may flag it; only the
  owner removes it.
- Before an artefact reaches the owner, diff it against the last revision they approved and
  report the fraction of their text surviving. This is cheaper than any round, and it was the
  only instrument that caught the deletions.
- Start implementation early against a validated core, and treat implementer STOPs as gate
  findings.
- Put "evaluate each cell's red and green before writing it" in the DISPATCH, not in the
  reviewer.
- Split a large spec into a small frozen core (what gates attack) and a measurement ledger
  (verified by re-running commands, not by re-reading). Commit artefacts at every round
  boundary.
- Contact caps and reserved classes: \[[review-economy]\].

Related: \[[review-economy]\] \[[reviewer-findings-are-hypotheses]\] \[[decision-tiers]\]

---
name: dont-review-a-moving-artefact
description: Before dispatching a reviewer/gate at an artefact, and while one is reading — making sure the thing reviewed is the thing that exists.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Freeze and hash the artefact before dispatching a review. Do not gate an artefact whose
author is still running. Hold commits on any path (or commit range) a live reviewer is reading.

**Why:**

- An orchestrator sent an author three corrections mid-run, took its FIRST return as the finish, and
  dispatched a reviewer. The author absorbed the corrections in a second round, growing the spec from
  +45 to +181 lines. The review opened on a version that no longer existed.
- Hours later: the orchestrator sent "context only, do not widen", the agent went idle, the reviewer
  was dispatched, and the file then moved again by +32 lines because the agent was still draining that
  message. An idle notice attests to the state when it was emitted.
- Committing a spec into an unrelated commit while a delta review was mid-round broke its premise
  ("nothing is committed"); it had to re-pin to a commit range.
- A brief said "the delta is A..B, one file". The orchestrator then landed three unrelated commits in
  that range. The spec itself was untouched, but the range now held three commits and six paths: the
  premise was void.

**How to apply:**

- Before gating: ask the author to confirm DONE and to report, not apply, anything in flight. The test
  is "idle since my last message to it, with nothing I sent still unabsorbed".
- A "context, do not widen" message is the dangerous kind: it costs time in the file, which is what
  collides with a reader.
- Name the artefact's own last-touching commit (`git log -1 --format=%H -- <path>`), not a range. A
  range is a claim about every file in it.
- Tell the reviewer: "nothing you read will be committed while you are live", and to check the hash
  first and stop on mismatch.
- When it happens anyway: commit the new state, send the reader a fresh pin (sha, md5, line count,
  what changed), tell it REJECT-on-process is costless, and say plainly it was your error.
- Your own push or landing between authoring a spec and dispatching against it stales the spec's
  push-state claims. State the invalidation in the brief.
- Dispatch a gate only after the last content edit. Do not let a sign-off message carry an
  instruction: separate messages, so nothing that closes a round can move the artefact.
- Anchor a gate on a committed revision. For an uncommitted artefact, use
  `git hash-object -w <file>` (an immutable blob id with no ref) and verify it with
  `git cat-file blob <id> | diff - <file>`.
- Gate side: snapshot `git status` at start and re-check before the verdict. On movement,
  halt, name the delta, and ask the hub.

Related: \[[reviewable-artefact]\] \[[writing-a-dispatch-brief]\] \[[peer-sessions]\]

---
name: writing-a-dispatch-brief
description: Before sending any prompt to a build, spec or review subagent — what every brief carries, what it must not, and the checks that catch the defects that ship in briefs
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Specify the PROPERTY, the forbidden shapes and the oracle; leave the MECHANISM to the agent
unless it is ruled ("this is ruled, not chosen"). Resolve every uncertainty before writing: the brief
carries conclusions and pointers, never reasoning. Read the finished brief as ONE document and ask of
each instruction whether another section forbids it. Premises: \[[brief-premises-are-hypotheses]\].

**Why:**

- A mechanism in a brief is a ceiling. Three agents each beat the mechanism handed to them, and said
  so: a structural invariant (parent options ⊆ child options on every inheritance edge) instead of a
  "fail if the count reverts" cell a pinned number could satisfy; one `git rev-parse --verify --quiet "<rev>^{commit}"` instead of a two-step check; a withdrawn claim instead of a re-aimed one ("replaces
  a false claim with a second false claim"). Checkable only because declared.
- 4 of 9 dispatches in one plan held thinking-out-loud ("WAIT", "ACTUALLY"); the failed one said
  "remove the flat fields" in its goal and "WAIT... keep them" in its body.
- The contradiction that ships is quieter: a correct premise beside a wrong instruction. Four in one
  session: a premise forbidding what the scope asked; "your report file only" next to an unscoped "push
  to main" (twelve unrelated commits pushed); a random token demanded inside pure Nix evaluation;
  "restate the dates" turning a marked quote into a paraphrase. A worktree fence made the spec's own
  two-file acceptance oracle unsatisfiable. A relayed gate exit required the very phrase the ruled
  repair deleted: a fixture built to identify a site is not a model of the repair.
- A review brief named three finding labels from the OTHER lane's report; "does the label exist"
  false-greened, because a report rejecting a label quotes it. Position discriminates: a real finding
  sits at a heading or table-row start. Six literal FAIL-IF phrases tripped on correctly preserved
  quotes of refuted claims.
- A class sweep given one exemplar shape found 5 wrong items, none of that shape. Authors fix the
  instance, not the class (the same lesson violated one section away three times). An author's
  "sections unchanged" list was wrong on 5 of 5 revisions checked, always overcounting.

**How to apply — every brief carries:**

---
name: defer-review-of-built-not-planned
description: When deciding whether a design review can wait until the system works
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Defer the deep review of what is already built until it runs. Do not defer the review of what is about to be built.

**Why:** The owner ruled "we'll deeply review design once we have a functional system, refactor is cheapish". That released a backlog in which almost all open rows rested on unreviewed design. It did not release the adversarial gate for NEW designs (spec, then gate, then validated, then implement), the "spec before development" rule, or the direct filing of measured defects.

The reason the gate survives is that "refactor is cheap" is a claim about the cost of change, not about detection. A defect that ships silently is never refactored, because nothing tells you it is there. In one arc the gate caught a diamond-shaped duplication that was exponential in output size. It was invisible to every test (the only fixture was a chain, and chains and sibling fan-ins are both trees) and it survived two adversarial rounds. The round-2 fix was verified to restore parity and was still wrong.

**How to apply:**

- Built and running: review against the running system.
- Not yet built: gate the spec before code.
- Include fixtures whose shape differs from a tree (diamonds, shared children) in any review of dedup or merge logic.

Related: \[[oracle-design]\] \[[nix-hidden-unsoundness]\]

---
name: spec-and-plan-before-code
description: Before any code change, and when moving from a written plan into multi-task execution.
type: workflow
---

**Rule:** Spec first and file the tracking task before touching code, including one-line changes.
After writing a plan, dispatch an INDEPENDENT plan reviewer before the first task. Execute with a
fresh agent per task and a two-stage review.

**Why:**

- A one-line change to public `gen-schema` (`_kind` on every instance) was measured green, committed and pushed with no spec. The
  owner rejected it on five design grounds (denormalisation, surface growth, non-totality on empty
  input, direction of contamination, re-nominalising a structural surface). It cost a public revert, a
  lock bump and three thrown-away fixture edits. Measurement answers "does it work"; the objections
  were "should it exist in this shape". The smallness made it feel exempt.
- The plan review was skipped twice. Cause: a seam between two skills. The plan-writing skill ends in
  SELF-review and a hard handoff; the execution skill reviews per task, not the whole plan.
- A correction that replicated: the content was fixed by measurement, but its EXTENT was not. A first
  grep found 3 sites, a second spelling found 3 more, a third spelling and an inherited direct call
  surfaced only at review. A change's blast radius is not derivable from its content.
- A plan with exact before/after code, executed by a fresh agent per task with two-stage review,
  shipped a 7-task, 25-file refactor with zero rework.

**How to apply:**

- Spec records rejected routes with reasons so later sessions cannot re-litigate them. Review the
  SPEC, then implement.
- When a correction replicates, the artefact to write and review is the SWEEP PREDICATE, with a
  liveness control on a known positive in a DIFFERENT spelling.
- Review chain: design review, spec review, PLAN review, per-task spec-compliance then quality review.
- Explore exhaustively before planning (exact paths, signatures, caller inventory). Plans carry
  concrete diffs and file references, not prose.
- Fresh worker per task with full context in the prompt. The coordinator applies 2-line review fixes
  itself rather than re-dispatching.
- Map the dependency chain so independent tasks run without blocking.
- Honour a requested checkpoint before a big mechanical grind even if the end state would be green;
  its value is catching a wrong turn before the cost is paid.
- When a worker reports "gaps I worked around", check whether the gap belongs at the source library.
  Re-run the gate yourself rather than accepting a worker's green.

Related: \[[reviewable-artefact]\] \[[review-economy]\] \[[writing-a-dispatch-brief]\]

---
name: suite-blind-on-its-classified-axis
description: Applies when reviewing a spec or test plan that was flagged with a risk class (ordering, identity, novel construction).
type: trap
---

**Rule:** When an artefact is classified under a review class, name the property that class protects,
then find the test that pins it. No such test is a finding, however green the suite.

**Why:** A collapse algorithm was classified "ordering semantics" because it decides by walk order which
arrival represents an element. Its spec said "first in walk order". A gate found no cell pinned that
choice: a build keeping the walk-LAST arrival passed every cell. Everything else was pinned; the one
free choice the mechanism makes had no oracle. The classification is a pointer to where to look, not a
ceremony tag.

**How to apply:**

- For each free choice the mechanism makes, write the mutant (e.g. last instead of first) and confirm
  some cell reds on it.
- Check controls pass at GREEN too: a control can be wrong like any predicate.

Related: \[[defect-reachable-by-two-paths]\] \[[assert-which-refusal-fired]\]

---
name: reviewer-findings-are-hypotheses
description: When acting on, relaying or filing an adversarial reviewer's findings, and when applying fixes from a review round
type: practice
---

**Rule:** A reviewer's finding is a hypothesis on exactly the same terms as an author's
claim. Re-derive it before building on it, and treat the FIX as the highest-risk surface of
the next revision.

**Why:**

- A gate asserted that renaming labels changes the emitted vertex order. The claim was
  transcribed faithfully into the next revision as the ground for a design choice. The next
  gate refuted it with one `nix eval`: order is invariant under label spelling. Neither party
  had run a probe that took seconds. Findings arrive wearing the authority of the adversarial
  process, so they get transcribed where an author's own claim would get checked.
- The fix for the severest finding of a round introduced a new mechanism defect. A false
  *reason* was replaced by a false *construction*.
- A remedy can be right while its severity argument is false. That is the dangerous
  combination, because the false "why" becomes load-bearing prose.
- A returning reviewer decays on text it has already approved. One gate found, in round 3,
  two defects present in round 1 text it had read line by line. Its own diagnosis: reading to
  check that corrections were absorbed is a different activity from reading to find what is
  wrong.
- A retraction that lands in a spec's body often fails to land in the copy filed as a ticket,
  and the ticket is what gets acted on.

**How to apply:**

- Relay evidence in a form that can be re-run: paste the command, not your summary of it.
  One paraphrase dropped an `--override-input` flag, and the gate then concluded the author
  had concealed the override.
- Write "the reviewer concludes X; I have not measured it" for any unmeasured severity.
- In the next dispatch, name the fixes as the primary review surface, and re-run each
  finding's own predicate across its whole class, not just at the sites the fix names.
- Ask a returning gate to list the sections it has now approved more than once, and point a
  fresh reader at those.
- Re-check a finding against the primary at filing time.
- Ask reviewers for retractions of refuted earlier findings, and record them with reasons, or
  the rejected version gets proposed again.
- If the gate is unavailable, record it as OWED. A third pass over your own reasoning is not
  an independent contact.

Related: \[[brief-premises-are-hypotheses]\] \[[gates-need-an-oracle]\] \[[conclusion-and-basis-are-two-findings]\]

- A red you cannot also produce on an unpatched copy of the same revision is not a finding.
  Prefer "my instrument moved" over "the library collapsed".

- Measure in the real checkout. If you need a copy, `git init` it or address it as
  `git+file://<path>?dir=ci`.

- Untracked files are invisible to flake evaluation. Use a guarded runner that refuses on
  git-unknown files, or `git add` first.

- A reviewer's "this field is dead/unread" is a hypothesis (a library may consume it internally);
  the gated suite run is the verification, so it has to actually gate.

Related: \[[ci-gate-discipline]\] \[[armed-controls]\] \[[success-signal-is-not-measurement]\]

Expect terse corrections ("Wrong repo." "Path-scope it." "That red is a finding."). Apply exactly
what is said and continue. When an approach goes wrong, say so and let the orchestrator revert;
narrowing scope after a revert beats repairing a bad approach. When told to match a pattern, read the
referenced files first.

## Hand off

Spec wrong or incomplete -> spec role (report the gap and stop). Need a measurement outside scope ->
scout. Landing needs judging -> gate.

Related: \[[roles-common-protocol]\] \[[role-gate]\] \[[role-spec]\]
Related: \[[presenting-a-decision]\] \[[before-asking-the-owner]\]

q15.query: What are the decision classification tiers used when filing tasks and architecture decisions?

results.text:
---
name: decision-tiers
description: When filing or picking up a change, to decide how much ceremony it gets (spec, gate, owner reading, design session)
type: practice
scope: local
---

**Rule:** Classify every change when it is filed, and write the class and a one-line reason in
the tracker body.

- **M, mechanical:** the outcome is fully determined by an existing ruling or spec, and a
  failure would be LOUD. The tracker body IS the spec (problem, mechanism, oracle). Execute it
  directly, with its own test and no gate round.
- **D, design:** creates or changes a construct, representation or public surface. Needs a
  lean spec, an adversarial gate, and an owner fork where one exists.
- **R, ruling-only:** the owner is the oracle. One reading, with no manufactured measurement.
- **N, new named thing** (a library, repository, roster member, user-facing surface or
  framework component): starts with a brainstorming session WITH the owner. A spec is
  dispatched only against the design that session approved.
  A change whose tier is unclear is D.

**Why:** Owner: "you're treating all decisions as equal… the overhead of ceremony has become a
risk unto itself." The N class came from two misses on one day. A framework spec was
dispatched within an hour of a ruling that meant "enter the design phase now", and the owner
had to stop it ("jumps the gun"). A tooling unit was re-homed three times after dispatch, each
time on a clarification the owner could have given in one sitting. Mechanism: no tier existed
for a new thing, so it fell into D, whose route is "dispatch a spec agent", and spec agents
read artefacts, not the owner. "An idle fleet is a dispatch trigger" also beat "ask early".

**How to apply:**

- The tell that the brainstorm was skipped: a spec whose open question is what the thing IS,
  where it LIVES, or what it is CALLED. Stop and hold the build.
- Brainstorm form: context first, one clarifying question at a time, two or three approaches
  with trade-offs, sections approved one by one.
- A forcing function licenses ENTERING a design phase, not skipping it. "Properly
  architected" means the document order: requirements, assessment, architecture, diagrams,
  then specs, then plans.
- An M task that hits an undecided design fork mid-execution STOPS and promotes itself.
- A design agent revising an owner-approved design does not reword an approved sentence. One
