  agent turned "closures never live in X" into "no closure is applied in X", which quietly
  revived an arm the owner had rejected. The dispatch says approved text is fixed, and asks for
  a sentence-level diff against the approval revision.
- The M tier removes the spec and the gate, not delegation (\[[delegate-authoring]\]).

Related: \[[before-asking-the-owner]\] \[[gates-need-an-oracle]\] \[[advance-on-reversible-defaults]\]

---
name: concurrency-budget
description: Before dispatching a subagent — how many may run at once, which model tier, and what to do when over the cap.
type: practice
scope: local
values:
  budget-strong-equivalents: owner-set 2026-10-14
  strong-to-mid-ratio: provisional
  agents-while-owner-present: provisional
---

**Rule:** Concurrency is a quota budget counted in strong-model equivalents (one strong-tier agent =
two mid-tier agents). Count what is live with `ListAgents` before every dispatch, and pass `model`
explicitly on every call. If you find yourself over the cap, stop dispatching and let it drain; do not
kill working agents.

**Why:**

- Agent definitions that set no model inherit the parent's (strongest) tier. Seven unqualified
  dispatches ran against a cap of four because the cap was never read. Every unqualified dispatch
  spends a strong slot.
- The orchestrator then stopped three lanes to get under the cap. The owner reversed it: "resume
  those agents ... they've already spent the tokens." The cap governs NEW spend; killing a running
  agent throws away paid work and buys nothing back.
- An old, too-low recorded cap caused the opposite failure: one lane running while four were allowed.
- A spike of 18 orphaned nix shells looked like a reason to lower the cap. The owner rejected that:
  the cause was agents dispatched against stalled or blocked tasks, spawning retries.

**How to apply:**

- Example budget of 6 equivalents: 6 strong, or 5 strong + 2 mid, or 4 strong + 4 mid.
- Model roles: the strongest model orchestrates (main session only: dispatch, verdicts, records). A
  strong model is the default worker for anything with judgement (implementation, review, audits,
  spec authoring). A cheap model only for purely mechanical sweeps (grep, listing, classification).
- A resume by message is a dispatch for cap purposes, on the agent's original tier. Prefer resuming a
  mid-tier lane for bounded one-line remedies when the strong tier is full.
- Before dispatching, confirm the task is actually unblocked and that no stalled peer still holds it.
- Name every agent `<task>-<role>` so the owner can track the fleet and you can address it.
- While the owner is present in a live decision session, keep it to 2-3 concurrent agents
  (\[[presenting-a-decision]\]).

Related: \[[resume-failed-agents]\] \[[one-writer-per-checkout]\] \[[presenting-a-decision]\]

---
name: delegate-authoring
description: When you are the orchestrator of a multi-agent session and are tempted to write specs, plans or sweeps yourself
type: practice
values:
  writer-revivals: provisional
---

**Rule:** The orchestrator keeps JUDGEMENT and delegates execution AND review. Spec, plan and
document authoring goes to fresh-context agents; the orchestrator's turns go to adjudicating
forks, synthesising verdicts, owner-in-the-loop decisions and tracker reconciliation.

**Why:** the orchestrator is the scarce, long-lived context. Every plan or spec written inline
burns tokens needed to hold the whole arc. Workers are cheap and disposable, and their context
resets. The owner flagged drift twice: once to a generic unnamed agent, and once to nearly
cutting independent plan review "for just aliases", which was a quality slip.

**How to apply:**

- Keep a named-role pipeline: scout → planner → INDEPENDENT plan review → writer → two-stage
  review → gate. Plan review is not skippable, even for extra-small tasks.
- Name agents by role. Use the stronger model for non-mechanical work.
- Small tasks may be planned inline. For anything complex, dispatch the author, review its
  output, and keep only the decision, not the prose.
- A mechanical tier removes ceremony, not delegation. The tell: you are hand-writing the
  third `sed` of a sweep.
- An auditor does not fix what it audits. A reviewer gets the artefact and the rubric, not the
  author's framing. Repairs go to a separate build dispatch.
- One agent per writable tree. Read-only agents may run concurrently.
- Namespace scratch files by work-item id. Sibling agents share the session scratchpad, and
  one agent's generic `run.sh` overwrote another's mid-run, destroying 68 of 80 measured rows.
  Commit the runner, so a collision cannot reach the recoverable copy.
- A revived writer has a round budget (about 3 or 4 revivals). After that, retire it and give
  a fresh author the artefact, the newest verdict and the written lessons list. One 17-round
  author reached about 1M tokens.
- Ask workers for terse output: no filler or hedging, but full sentences.

Related: \[[writing-a-dispatch-brief]\] \[[decision-tiers]\] \[[agent-report-delivery]\]

- Graph construction (Mokhov): `empty vertex vertices overlay overlays connect edge edges path circuit star clique tree forest gmap induce transpose hasVertex hasEdge removeVertex removeEdge`.
- `buildRoots { parentGraph; importGraph; edgeGraphs; decls; types; kinds; strict ? true; }` ->
  `{ nodes; nodeOrder; kinds; }` (`buildNodes` is a tombstone). `P` and `I` labels are reserved.
- Evaluators: `eval { parseParent; prior; decision; provenance; declaredDependencies; } attributes scope`
  (an options door: unknown keys refused by name); `evalDebug` (cycle tracing, defeats memoization);
  `evalWarm { … } { scope; attributes; prior; decision; }`.
- Accessor record: `node`, `get` (tier 1); `allNodes`, `allNodeIds`, `allNodesWhere`, `subtreeOf`,
  `nodesOfType` (tier 2, force the tree); plane interface `facade`, `resolutional`, `served`,
  `structuralEdges`, `decisionFindings`, `projectionFindings`.
- Plane interface: `structural name` (total partition), `resolutionalNames`, `edgePrefix` (`"edges-"`),
  `coldDecision`, `mkDecision { isClean; reusable; }`, `mkFacade`.
- Combinators (`self: id: value`): `shadow`, `inherit'`, `inheritAll`, `inheritSet`, `circular { carrier = { bottom; leq; height; quotient; }; } step`, `collectionAttr { } traverse extract`, `collectImports`,
  `collect`/`collectByType` (no `id` argument), `followEdge`, `collectByLabel`, `subtypeOf`. Queries
  (`self` first): `parent children childrenIds ancestors descendants siblings isAncestor isDescendant nodesByType`.
- Resolution calculus: `resolve { wf; dataFilter; mode ? "reachable"; order; group | groupBy; bound; direction ? "outbound"; } self from`; `wellFormed`, `labelOrder`, preset `neron` (`parent* imports?`,
  D < I < P). Modes: `reachable`, `witnesses`, `visible` (with `shadowed`, `single`).
- Engine: `mkRule { pos; neg; } head`, `mkProgram rules`, `leastModel seed program` (routes via `armFor`
  to `leastModelUnary`/`leastModelRounds`), `reduct`, `wellFoundedModel interpretation program`,
  `verdictNames`, `Pos`, `solve interpretation program` (adds `condensationDepth`, `provenance`),
  `foldContributions`, `verifiedDepth`, `acceptanceSignal`.
- Minting: `mintStrata kinds emitters -> { nodes; edges; strata; unrun; sites; }`, `argumentBinding`.
- Cascade: `mkKind { below; resolve; spawns; nta; dedupKey; fold; kindValue; } name`, `mkKinds`
  (ordered fold), `mkClaim`, `resolveClaims { ctx ? {}; } kinds claims -> { resources; wiring; unrun; trace; }`; `folds.{ same one list mergeAttrs byKey }` (signature `key: [v]: v`).
- `stratify { schedule; stratumOf; within; seed; advance; describe; }`; `foldEquations { settings ? {}; } { scope; parseParent; schedule; declaredDependencies; }` -> an 11-field sealed context.

## Invariants

| tier                | what                                                  | ceremony                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| M (mechanical)      | purely mechanical, clear resolution                   | the item body is the spec; ships with its own test; no gate round                                                                                                             |
| D (design)          | a design choice                                       | spec + tracker item before code, then a gate                                                                                                                                  |
| R (ruling)          | needs an owner ruling                                 | spec + tracker item before code                                                                                                                                               |
| N (new named thing) | a new library, repo, user-facing surface or component | owner brainstorm FIRST (context, one question at a time, 2-3 approaches with trade-offs, sections approved one by one); a spec is dispatched only against the approved design |

Unclear tier = D. Tell that an N brainstorm was skipped: a spec whose open question is what the
thing IS, where it lives, or what it is called.

## 6. Filing, reports and gates

- File a tracker item only for a component or a ruling. Docs drift (counts, prose, citation
  anchors, README) is fixed in the landing that finds it: no item, no report.
- One report per landing. One gate contact by default; a second needs a reserved class
  (a refutation, a novel construction, identity/ordering of the substrate); a third is a spec
  defect that goes to the owner or is dropped.
- Spec oracles split: the GATING oracle ships with the landing; the GUARANTEE (exhaustive suites,
  planted violations, censuses) is filed deferred and re-armed once a consumer proves the value.

## 7. Owner readings and blocked rows

---
name: filing-caps
description: When deciding whether to file a tracker item, write a report, split oracles, or route an owner ask
type: practice
scope: local
values:
  reports-per-landing: owner-set 2026-09-16
---

**Rule:** File a tracker item only for a COMPONENT or a RULING. Write one report per landing.
Batch owner readings into one periodic sitting. Every owner ask gets a tracker row the day it
is made, wired to what it gates.

**Why:** over eight days, the framework route landed (7 of 8 items, bar blockers down from 54
to 6), while the backlog stayed flat (155 filed / 152 closed), report files doubled to 78 a
day, and the planning map grew to 3,649 lines and needed agents just to read it. Separately, an
early owner ask (visualisation tooling) never became a row, so a query-derived frontier could
never surface it. An ask with no row vanishes.

**How to apply:**

- Before filing, ask "component or ruling?" Docs counts, prose sites, citation anchors, README
  drift and stale comments are fixed in the landing that finds them: no ticket, no report, no
  handoff line.
- **Value/guarantee split.** A spec's oracles split into a GATING oracle (the mechanism driven
  red and read, plus the consumer's evaluation green), which ships with the landing, and the
  GUARANTEE (property cells, planted violations, censuses, enforcers), which is filed as one
  deferred row per component and re-armed once the consumer proves the value. Builders land
  value only.
- **One unit, one session:** a unit lands in one dispatch with its integration arm green, or
  it is split. It is not carried over.
- A user-facing surface exits on the OWNER having run it, not on agents' green.
- Readings that wait for the sitting take the recommendation meanwhile, marked "defaulted,
  reversible".
- **A row truly blocked on the owner is WIRED, not narrated:** give it a `blocks` edge to the
  single open sitting row, and remove the edge in the act that banks the ruling. Then the ready
  list shows only agent-actionable work. At a sitting's close, re-link only what was
  intentionally deferred.
- After banking an ask, RUN the query that derives the agenda and confirm the row appears
  (\[[tracker-body-writes]\]).
- Carrier rows that get regenerated restate their body (current state only, size-capped) and
  move superseded text to a ledger file.
- Keep a trap-list entry only where a tool's zero would otherwise read as an absence.

Related: \[[review-economy]\] \[[integration-validates]\] \[[durable-records-not-handoffs]\]

- `declaration { pos?; neg?; label?; promote?; when?; } relata head`. No body means a FACT. `label`
  names the edge the head denotes; `promote` (a relation kind) makes the head a NODE with labelled-tuple
  relata. `when` is the literal tier: `has a` to `pos`, `not (has a)` to `neg`, `all` conjoins; `any`,
  `eq`, and functions are refused, and `when` beside `pos`/`neg` is refused.
- `rule decl`; `program frozen declarations` (refuses a relatum no earlier pass settled);
  `unresolvedRelata` (that refusal's content as data, because `tryEval` discards messages).
- `model { program; interpretation; complete; prior; }` (all required): solves this pass from scratch.
  `prior` is the omission guard: refuses when a prior rule is missing. A first pass states
  `prior = null`. `interpretation` is a list of `{ atom; verdict; }` assertions for this pass only.
- The result record: `trueAtoms withheldAtoms undefinedAtoms falseAtoms` (partition program atoms plus
  asserted ones), `verdict`, `resolve`, `adjudication`, `complete`, `converged`, `provenance`,
  `condensationDepth`, and `rules` (keyed by the JSON of each canonical rule, sorted and deduped).
- `ruleEdges model decls -> { candidates; reached; promotions; promoted; }`; `mkModel` (its `__contract`
  lists required fields).
- `flagNames`/`flags`: van Antwerpen's `T`/`P`/`U`. `adjudicate { program; model; interpretation; }`,
  `stableModelCriterion`, `adjudicationOutcomes` (`admitted refused not-evaluated`), `stableModelBudget`
  (a derived figure with its derivation, never a bare number).
- Policy-body algebra: `body { name; clauses; declared; }` (`declared` is required; `null` = open
  world), `emit`, `forEach { over; emit; }`, door clauses `{ when?; body = ref r; emits; binds; suppresses; }`, `ctorNames` (`member deliver edge suppress realize`), `deriveCodomain` (takes no
  context, which proves no fact depends on firing context), `groundInstances { door ? null; sources ? {}; } context body`, `codomainBreaches contract decls`, `admit`. `escape`/`fireEscape` are retired
  aliases that refuse, naming the gen-rules door.

## Invariants

q16.query: Why are silent fallbacks such as or [] considered harmful when looking up required attributes?

results.text:
---
name: silent-fallbacks-delocalise-failures
description: When a change produces a surprisingly large failure cascade, when reviewing `or []`/`or null`/warn-and-continue code, or when a rename lands.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** A fallback that substitutes a plausible value for a missing one moves the failure away from
its cause and multiplies it. The observed blast radius is the fallback's shape. Find the fallback
before believing the count.

**Why:**

- Dropping one override broke an aspect lookup; the lookup took a warn path to an EMPTY value, and
  evaluation died far downstream on an unrelated assertion. Reported radius: 42 cells. With the lookup
  pointed at the right field (one line), the real cost was 3 cells, one assertion, zero hard errors.
- A field rename hit four consumer sites. One read it bare and aborted loudly. Three read it through
  `or [ ]` and kept working with an empty chain: a selection predicate that always held and a
  provenance hierarchy that silently flattened. The crash was the cheap half.
- A dispatch guard keyed on destructured argument names silently never fired when a stale name was not
  in scope. No error; an entire downstream configuration came out empty.

**How to apply:**

- Diagnosing: on a big cascade, look upstream for one place that answered "missing" with a value
  instead of a refusal. Fix it, re-measure, and report the post-fix figure as the radius, with the
  cascade noted separately.
- Designing: before adding `or [ ]`, `or null` or warn-and-continue, name what it makes unobservable.
  Fallback is right where absence is legitimate, wrong where absence means a broken contract. Where
  both apply, put the fallback at exactly one place, the ingestion boundary.
- Reviewing: treat warn-and-return-empty as a finding. The warning rides on a value nobody forces.
- After a rename or contract change, audit the sites that did NOT break. A hard read fails in CI; an
  `or` default ships.
- Guards that filter silently (argument-presence dispatch) need a positive control showing they fire.

Related: \[[fix-the-producer-first]\] \[[armed-controls]\]

---
name: fix-the-producer-first
description: When a defect shows up at many consumers, or a fix is proposed that teaches N readers to work around something.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Look at the producer before guarding the consumers. A value that misdescribes its own
constructor is the defect; N defensive readers are a repair.

**Why:** A recommended fix had every gen `typeMerge` export learn to see past a partner's functor. The
owner asked to "consider this more deeply from the other side" and to scout first. Re-derived from the
producer: `gen-schema`'s `refined` presented its BASE type's functor (copying nixpkgs' `addCheck`
shape to buy parity), so every functor-keyed reader correctly took it for the bare base. Making the producer honest, plus ONE
explicit reader of a declared base, measured zero regressions three times over and was cheaper.
A consumer-side guard places a permanent obligation on every reader, and copying an upstream shape
for parity can import the upstream's own accident.

**How to apply:**

- Before recommending an arm that changes N readers, ask whether the thing they read describes itself
  truthfully. If not, put the producer-side arm first.
- Price the producer arm's unmeasured premise with a scout rather than recommending around it.
- Prefer a construction that makes the defect impossible over a repair of a bad intermediate.
- Do not borrow a nearby rule by name: a rule about the threat model (caller mistakes) is not a rule
  about self-misdescription.

Related: \[[silent-fallbacks-delocalise-failures]\] \[[arms-that-should-not-be-offered]\]

- `children`/`derived-children`/`imports`/`edges-<l>`/`marks` are reserved names nothing supplies: declare
  them in `attributes`. A materialization without `children` refuses by name (it used to return a silent
  partial tree). `self.get id "children"` excludes `derived-children`.
- `followEdge "X"` reads a computed attribute `edges-X`; `buildRoots` only writes `decls.__edges.X`.
- `star` runs leaves to center (inverted relative to Mokhov), matching child-to-parent `P`.
- `subtypeOf`'s default `eq` compares nothing; a value-comparing `eq` drags in the synthetic `__edges`.
- `allNodes` loses walk order (attrset); use `allNodeIds`. Root ties break by **bytewise codepoint**, and
  `derived-children` interleave with `children`. A flat fixture cannot tell the two orders apart.
- The import relation is protected by its **name**: a renamed import attribute is served stale.
- `circular` refuses three causes separately (bad declaration, non-ascending step, height exceeded).
- `resolve` here is the Néron specificity function, unrelated to the gen-resolve library.
- A rule with two literals can be **unary**: routing uses the greatest positive body arity.
- `tryEval` discards a throw's message, so refusal text is unreadable in-language.
- **Two abort signatures:** an unforced accumulator chaining through function application exhausts
  `max-call-depth`; through a bare `+` it overflows the C stack. A sweep armed for one reads the other as
  green. A strict read forces only the field it reads.
- Cascade `wiring` is total: test key membership, then read. A bare `wiring.<id>.entries` aborts
  uncatchably on an unregistered subject; `(wiring.<id> or { entries = []; })` erases the difference.
- A resolver returning a list, number or `null` used to contribute nothing silently; the answer is now
  shape-checked. Keep a `{ }` live control for the legitimate empty answer.
- `folds.same` refuses functions and paths before comparing (`==` on functions depends on sharing and
  on the evaluator, \[[nix-tryeval-and-equality]\], and `toJSON` on a path aborts or copies it into the store).
- Mint: a same-run relatum at the same pass refuses with a message that reads like a typo. Reading one
  result field runs the whole mint. `strata` counts distinct passes.
- `stratify` throws nowhere; a list field is forced to its spine only, so `settled = [ (throw …) ]` may
  never fire.
- Do not cite a paper you do not hold as the source of a construction; mark the attribution unchecked.

- Silent failures (absence claims, greps, counters, a cost blowup returning the right answer) need
  controls. Loud failures (suite red, build break, named refusal, even an uncatchable abort) need none.
  Classify by whether anything REPORTS the failure, not by how bad it is.
- **Reserved classes** get a second contact by default: security boundaries; data loss or migration;
  concurrency; public interface compatibility; and the project's own classes (here: substrate identity
  or ordering semantics, refutations of standing results, novel constructions entering the substrate).
  Otherwise exit after one construction-clean contact; a second round only as a bounded delta check.
- Track escapes: defects found after a unit has exited review. If more than 1 in 10 gated units
  escape, raise the default to two contacts. This is guidance, not an enforced gate.
- **Exit by byte-identity transfer:** prove the mechanism surface unchanged (a digest or tree diff,
  measured in the verdict), transfer the earlier instruments, verify only the delta.
- **Third contact:** a fresh design agent gets the document, every report and owner rulings as
  premises, reworks the whole, and a fresh reviewer takes contact 1. Do not override the cap for "one
  final review".
- The finding gate drafts owner-facing amendment text in its verdict; one fresh reviewer checks it. The
  drafter does not review its own draft.
- **Reports are FILES** at a versioned path (`reports/<item>-<role>-v0.md`, bumped per round). The
  message carries verdict, findings table, anchors and path; the verdict line also lands in the tracker
  body. Artefacts travel as files, not relay prose; spans are machine-extracted, not retyped;
  appliers match content, not coordinates.
- A new instrument proves its armed control once, at introduction, in-tree. Recurring tool faults
  become tooling fixes, not more warnings.
- Counts downstream of a batch's own edits are stale by construction: re-derive at the landing rev.
  Stale counts during a retirement wave are churn; fix one only when touching the surface or when a
  decision rests on it. Formatting churn is not a risk class.
- For reference-grade libraries, deletion needs a domain argument; a usage count is not a ground.
- Process changes run as a trial with an explicit acceptance number, recorded where tracked.
- The teeth do not lighten: construction findings block unconditionally; gates use fresh contexts and
  armed controls.

Related: \[[gates-need-an-oracle]\] \[[filing-caps]\] \[[relay-through-the-hub]\] \[[spec-and-plan-before-code]\] \[[armed-controls]\]

---
name: tested-path-equals-shipped-path
description: When a project's CI exercises a different resolution path, evaluator or input wiring than its users
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Find out which path your users actually take, and make CI exercise that path, under every evaluator you claim to support.

**Why / measured:**

- A framework that declares no flake inputs resolves its library hub through a `fetchTarball` fallback that reads a rev from a template's lockfile. Its own CI used the flake-input path. The two paths carried different transitive library revisions from one pin, so a consumer hit a throw that a 1221-cell suite could not see.
- A narrow sub-flake without the input did exercise the fallback. Eight cells there caught an old-pin/new-wiring mismatch that the flake arm read as 4/4 green. A bump validated only by `--override-input hub/member` can never turn that arm green, because the fallback reads the lock node directly.
- Local development ran one Nix evaluator while CI ran another with lazy trees on. A flake input's path text is a per-evaluation virtual path under lazy trees, so a minting defect was green locally and red in CI. The owner then required every library to work under all three major evaluators (upstream Nix, Determinate and Lix), with exact pins kept at the latest release and a staleness reader that turns a pin red when it falls behind.

**How to apply:**

- For a fallback-resolving project, also verify bumps on a consumer template that declares no input (`nix flake check --override-input <framework> .`).
- Every acceptance oracle names all evaluators. A result that differs between evaluators is a defect unless the divergence is stated.
- Note per-evaluator quirks. For example, one evaluator's `flake check` does not force devShells, so evaluate them explicitly.

Related: \[[confirm-baseline-before-claiming-a-gap]\] \[[nix-which-flake-which-output]\]

- Options are closed and refused by name; `dispatch`'s operand record is open but missing fields refuse.
- In `functionArgs` polarity, **`false` means REQUIRED**.
- A `groupOrder` of length ≤ 1 never consults `r.group` and skips cross-group validation: everything
  lands under that one name. `groupOrder = [ ]` fires nothing, silently.
- `extract` / `combine` default to NO threading: a cascade needs both or the downstream group never fires.
- Empty groups are ABSENT from `.actions`; read with `or [ ]`.
- Override suppression is forward only: a later group cannot suppress an earlier group's fired rule.
- `exclusive` keeps top priority per group, not globally.
- A rule with `produces != null` skips classify-validation and may emit foreign-group actions
  silently; `produces = [ ]` counts as declared while `deriveGroup` leaves `group = null`.
- `mkActions` reserves `classify` and `groupOfKind`: a tag with either name is silently shadowed.
  Constructor `args` can overwrite `__action`. `classify` on an untagged value throws uncatchably.
- A `chain` result is not a `mkRule` record (no `group`): multi-group dispatch fails with a raw
  missing-attribute error. Its identity is `null` if either arm is anonymous; `override` throws on an
  anonymous original. `restrict` prefixes identity with `restricted:`.
- `fromFunctionMatch` ignores `id` entirely: an id-conditional rule matches every id. `mkMatch` reads
  `id` but expects gen-select's five-accessor context, not the flat dispatch context.
- `mkMatch` unwraps only ONE `__restricted` level; `fromFunctionMatch` recurses.
- `selectorSpecificity` scores `entity` / `kind` / `coord` as 0, and `any` sums branches like `and`.
- CI's gen-select pin may be older than current gen-select; the adapter's tested surface is narrower.
- The repo was renamed from gen-derive. When grepping for residue of a rename, exclude the file that
  records the rename (it is tracked, so `git grep` sees it).

Related: \[[gen-overview]\] \[[gen-algebra]\] \[[gen-retired]\]

---
name: scope-every-universal
description: Before finalising design prose or a report — every "every/any/always/never/only/cannot", and the one sentence that decides what the report is about.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Treat every universal quantifier in your own draft as a defect until you have scoped it.
And find the framing sentence of every report (its scope, its owner, what is out of play) and ask
what measurement would falsify it.

**Why:**

- Three claims failed in one spec arc, each after the work had been done correctly: "reachable ONLY
  through `get`" (the accessor also exposed raw records); "a value the type does NOT admit" (the
  language has no static types); "byte-parity holds for EVERY possible decision" (false on a second
  axis). The narrow claim was true every time and was stated wide. Twice the wide claim contradicted
  another clause, once making an oracle look pointless.
- "Our CI exercises the flake path only" was repeated to a peer and banked. False: one template
  declared no such input, so eight cells ran the fallback path, and those were the cells that caught a
  break the main path read green on.
- "The library ships no X by design, so injecting X is not available" was true of the library and
  settled nothing: the consumer had X. It rode inside a rigorous report and decided who owned the
  defect.
- A pass found a real stale table and invented a mechanism to explain it. The mechanism was banked as
  law before review; review refuted it on the document's own text. The observation needed no defence;
  the mechanism did.

**How to apply:**

- For each universal: what is the widest thing this now says? Narrow it to the axis you established,
  or name the excluded axis in the same breath. Prefer "over axis X, ..." to "always".
- Where a construction protects one axis and not another, say which and why. An unqualified safety
  claim reads as "no oracle needed".
- Self-check: grep your draft for the quantifier words and re-read each at its widest.
- Report framing tells: an absolute over a corpus ("only", "every", "no consumer"); a true but
  irrelevant "X cannot do Y" offered as if it answered "can Y be done". Measure it or mark it as an
  assumption.
- An explanation that arrives WITH a measurement and generalises it into a law is the thing to review
  hardest. Ask what the law would have predicted the day before.

Related: \[[armed-controls]\] \[[counts-need-anchor-and-population]\]

---
name: nix-laziness-design
description: When designing Nix code that crosses scopes, holds configs in state, or validates module arguments
type: practice
---

**Rule:** In Nix, the invariant is usually "no FORCE", not "no REFERENCE". Hold lazy references freely, force deliberately and shallowly, and prefer a loud infinite-recursion error to a silent wrong answer.

**Why / measured:**

- Cross-host config-thunk resolution looked like it needed a new stratum and an engine. A spike showed that `evalModules`' own lazy fixpoint co-evaluates: an acyclic use resolves, and a genuine cycle throws a loud, uncatchable recursion. "No silent cycle" strictly dominates the older stratum design, which was silently wrong on the circular case.
- A reviewer claimed that reading an aggregate an app also emits into is cyclic. It is not: emission and consumption are different attributes, and per-attribute laziness handles it. The invariant to enforce is narrower: emission must never read the aggregate.
- An effects runtime `deepSeq`ed its state, forcing every option default of any config object held there. Wrapping the value as `_: value` hides it (`deepSeq` skips lambdas). Store keys, not configs, where only presence matters. This applies to that runtime only; do not carry the fear to designs without the deep force.
- Threading `_: value` closures with `prev // {...}` per step made forcing the final map chain through every closure (5660 frames, stack overflow). Forcing only the top-level spine each step (`builtins.seq (attrNames m) m`) collapsed the depth to O(1) and kept bodies lazy.
- A collision validator forced `config._module.args` at collection time and recursed through the `evalModules` it was checking. Keep validators lazy. The consequence is that errors then surface only when `warnings` are forced.
- An `mkIf` gate can gate config but cannot conditionally declare an option: that would need `imports ← guard(options) ← options ← imports`.
- Key maps by identity hash, not by coordinates: function-valued declarations break JSON serialization.
- Emits forced during assembly must self-gate as a list (`optionals (pathExists f) [...]`), or a missing file throws fleet-wide.

Related: \[[nix-hidden-unsoundness]\] \[[nix-tryeval-and-equality]\] \[[flake-parts-transposition-limit]\]
Related: \[[presenting-a-decision]\] \[[before-asking-the-owner]\]

q17.query: How should container images be referenced in deployment manifests and configurations?

results.text:
---
name: pin-container-images-by-digest
description: When adding or bumping a container image in Nix-managed Kubernetes manifests.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Reference container images through the repo's tracked image-metadata files and a digest
accessor, not an inline tag. Let the updater tool re-resolve digests.

**Why:** An inline tag can name an image that does not exist. A deploy broke with `ImagePullBackOff`
because a GitHub *release* tag had no matching *container* tag; the registry only published a rolling
`develop` tag. A digest-pinned entry that an updater bumps makes even a rolling tag safe.

**How to apply:**

- One metadata file per image (name, tag, digest, hash, arch, os), at a path keyed `<ns>/<name>`.
  The manifest reads `image = { inherit (images."<ns>/<name>") repository digest; }`, which renders
  `repository@sha256:...` with no tag.
- Check the tool's output path. One updater's `init` wrote a three-level path that included the
  registry, which broke the two-level fold into accessor keys. Move the file, then verify the accessor
  resolves with `nix eval`.
- Single-segment official images (`alpine`) also break a two-level layout; use `library/<name>`.
- Validate that a rolling tag exists cheaply before the heavy init: `skopeo inspect docker://<ref>`.
- A tool that runs via `nix run .#tool` evaluates the whole flake first. One broken module mid-batch
  silently kills every later step, so fix eval before continuing. `git add` new metadata files
  before any eval, because flakes ignore untracked files.
- When the full environment build is already red for an unrelated reason, validate in isolation
  (evaluate the image-ref set and the rendered container image fields) and say so.

Related: \[[nix-flake-hygiene]\] \[[infra-changes-owner-deploys]\]

---
name: infra-changes-owner-deploys
description: When a change touches live infrastructure config (host configs, secrets, cluster manifests) — agents author and commit, the owner approves and deploys.
type: practice
scope: local
---

**Rule:** An agent may author and commit infrastructure-config changes like any other build, but it
never runs a switch, deploy or rollout to a live host. Deployment is the owner's act. Secrets follow
the same split: the agent wires the mechanism, the owner decides what root-of-trust material exists.

**Why:** An infra change (a session hook, a packaged tool, a service) alters the environment every
later session runs in. Holding such work back as "unauthorised" stalls it; deploying it from a
session removes the owner's last checkpoint. The split keeps both: work flows, deploys stay human.

**How to apply:**

- Author and commit under the repo's normal conventions (linear history, module conventions). The
  report names the change for approval and says "deployment owed by the owner".
- Secrets: always use the repo's declared generators (for example `agenix generate` with
  agenix-rekey). Hand-encrypt only values issued externally, and document the provisioning procedure
  next to the declaration. Hand-rolled values fork provenance from the generators.
- A human-held master credential (the password that unlocks the vault the other secrets are recovered
  from) does not go into the repo, even encrypted. Encrypting it does not change what it is: it
  collapses a trust tier that exists only because it is held out of band. Build the consuming
  mechanism self-gated on the file's presence (`builtins.pathExists`) so it is fully inert without
  it, and never create the file. Offer a credential-free alternative.
- Do not generalise the credential rule to every root of trust. A CA root encrypted to a hardware key
  in the repo was ruled acceptable. Ask rather than extend a security ruling by analogy.
- In a public infra repo, keep PR bodies and commit messages free of IPs, CIDRs, real hostnames,
  domains, ports and operational counts. See \[[public-artifact-hygiene]\].

Related: \[[public-artifact-hygiene]\] \[[pin-container-images-by-digest]\]

---
name: nixos-module-conventions
description: When writing modules in a personal or fleet NixOS/home-manager configuration repository with established conventions
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Internalise the repository's idioms from its existing exemplars before writing. Do
not invent structure. Owner: "if I have to give you explicit instructions I may as well make
the modifications myself."

**Why:** a set of modules that ignored the project's conventions was tech debt the owner had to
clean up. Each convention below was learned from a correction or a breakage.

**How to apply:**

- **One concern per file.** Split a multi-facet feature (daemon and firewall / its secret /
  platform-specific parts), and open each file with a 1–2 line header naming its concern. Do not
  write a kitchen-sink file mixing home, system and secrets.
- **Presence is a role decision, not an `enable` toggle.** To turn a feature off fleet-wide,
  remove it from the role's includes. Settings parameterise the behaviour of an included
  feature; they never gate whether it exists.
- **Paths come from schema fields, not hand-built.** Anything forced during the BASE flake
  evaluation (schema and registry option defaults) cannot reference `self`: registry → `self`
  → flake outputs → registry recurses infinitely. Use a path literal such as `rootPath = ../..`
  there.
- **Make runtime files on REMOTE hosts real store-path dependencies.**
  `toString (rootPath + "/x.crt")` makes the whole flake source the dependency, which a remote
  deploy tool did not copy, so it worked only on the build host. Use
  `"${builtins.path { path = …; name = "x.crt"; }}"`.
- **Centralise generators and policies in their designated files**, and wire them through the
  documented include points. Fix a missing import; do not inline a copy.
- **Per-user content that needs a system resource** is a user-scoped module with a per-class
  branch, not a host-scoped loop over users.
- **Emit into the collector pools** (persistence, cache) that the repository provides, rather
  than writing the final option directly.
- **Locality over indirection.** Do not create a shared constants or `_lib.nix` file for a
  handful of values. A trivial one-line expression repeated at a few sites beats a helper file.
  The legitimate shared abstraction is a schema field.
- Format with the repository's `nix fmt <files>` (\[[format-before-commit]\]).

Related: \[[format-before-commit]\] \[[by-construction-over-repair]\]

---
name: gen-view
description: Working in gen-view, the substrate's derived-view constructor (view definitions as data, materialized view relations over scope graphs).
type: reference
verified: unverified
---

**Purpose:** the substrate's **derived-view constructor**. A view *definition* is plain data; a view
*relation* is the named result of materializing it over a scope graph. Registry, topology, channel, role
and movement are **one construction** at three key shapes (`movement` ≡ `channel`; `registry` ≡ `role`
modulo a field name). Do not "differentiate" them to make a tidier claim true. In the framework, this is
how content moves along edges and how queryable derived relations are held.

**Status:** provisional container. The *library* name is temporary (its constructs will fold into a
larger library as a sublibrary); the *construct* names are permanent and each is grounded at a primary
source. Do not weaken a construct name because the container is provisional.

**Depends on:** gen-prelude, gen-graph (`lib` is a function of both). gen-scope is a **ci-only** input:
the query authority (`engine`) is injected as a field, which keeps `lib/` evaluator-free. A test
asserts that absence over `lib/` with a positive control. Do not "simplify" by importing the authority.
**Inherited:** most of the surface arrived by retirement of gen-edge (the `(S,T,P,M)` content-movement
algebra, Kahn-ordered materialization, the trace/`hashTrace` oracle cluster) and gen-pipe (channels,
map/filter/fold/route operators, provenance). Bind the names here; route no work to the archived repos.
Some surfaces did **not** arrive (source re-walk, a producer `contribute`, `deferred`); minting one is a
design decision, not a lookup.
**Not its job:** answering questions without holding structures (gen-select), the labelled walk and Kahn's
algorithm (gen-graph; composed, never reimplemented), minting (gen-identity).

## API (by layer)

---
name: gen-link
description: Working in gen-link, cross-flake aspect federation (normalize, origin-stamp, disjoint union, facet wiring, resolution manifest).
type: reference
---

**Purpose:** federate aspect registries from several flakes into one graph.
`link { wire ? {}; } sources` normalizes each registry into an origin-free includes-graph, stamps every
node with a federation ORIGIN, disjoint-unions the subgraphs, mints every merged node's identity through
gen-scope's staged minting entry (each facet filling is a relatum), and returns a diffable resolution
manifest. gen-link owns only the origin coordinate, the union-with-relabel and the manifest; it delegates
every computation to a sibling. A node is NAMED by its identifier (`"b/apps/app"`, origin-qualified);
its IDENTITY is a derived content address carried as a field. gen-link mints nothing.

**Depends on / used by:** root inputs gen-prelude, gen-scope, gen-view, gen-schema, gen-algebra,
gen-aspects (gen-merge only in `ci/`). Used by the hub (re-exported as `link`) and `examples/demo`.
Not its job: minting (gen-scope `mintStrata`, gen-schema), aspect payload and keys (gen-aspects),
edge resolution (gen-view `referenceResolution`), materialization (gen-view), record algebra
(gen-algebra), building registries (gen-merge), graph queries (gen-graph), domain vocabulary (every facet
and class key arrives per source in `keySemantics`), writing a lock file (the consumer does).

**Future grammar (ruled, not built):** federated references will be kind-qualified,
`namespace.<kind>.name`, so cross-kind collisions are inexpressible. Today ships the two-segment
origin-qualified form; do not take it as settled.

**Layout (`lib/`):** `ref.nix` (parseRef, origins), `normalize.nix`, `rewrite.nix` (originStamp/alias),
`union.nix`, `facets.nix`, `contract.nix`, `manifest.nix`, `link.nix` (the conductor). Root `default.nix`
is a function, `import ./gen-link { }`, with formals `prelude scope view schema algebra aspects`
defaulting to lock pins.

**API:**

---
name: deploy-success-is-not-live
description: When confirming that a NixOS/microVM/home deploy actually changed the running system
type: trap
verified: unverified
---

**Rule:** A green deploy proves the new configuration was built and activated somewhere, not that the running process uses it. Check the thing that is running.

**Why / measured:**

- Deploying a microVM parent host repoints `/var/lib/microvms/<guest>/current` at the new runner but does not restart the guest. The activation log, `systemctl is-active microvm@<guest>` and "Activation successful" were all green while the guest ran the old config.
- The parent's system closure does not contain the guest's unit files, so grepping the parent toplevel for a guest flag reads 0 while the flag is present. `nix store diff-closures` between parent generations shows only `source`, however large the guest change.
- An activation does not restart a unit whose definition did not change. An ownership fix outside the unit file needed a manual restart.
- After a deploy, the running shell kept its old alias, which baked in an old store path. It went on using the old binary until a fresh shell was opened.
- `is-active` reads `active` for a crash-looping unit too.

**How to apply:**

- microVMs: compare `readlink -f .../current` with `readlink -f .../booted`. If they differ, the change is not live: `systemctl restart microvm@<guest>`. Inspect `/var/lib/microvms/<guest>/toplevel` for guest content.
- Read the journal, not `is-active`, for unit health.
- Open a fresh shell after changing aliases or wrappers.
- Deploys to shared hosts are the owner's act unless explicitly delegated.

Related: \[[per-machine-state]\]

- Every record-taking step is a `prelude.door`: unknown options are refused by name, catchably, with the
  contract published as data (`__contract`).
- One override rule: the lowest priority number wins, and ties merge. nixpkgs' order pass is DROPPED.
- One crossing site to the foreign protocol (`defineType`), so one type value serves both engines. A gen
  type states itself in gen's own words (`verify`, `admits`, `typeMergeRel`, `carries`) and gets nixpkgs
  field names only when exported.
- A redeclared option is decided by the TYPE ALGEBRA, never by position. A non-merging pair is a named
  refusal listing every declaring file.
- A container is recognised by its fold and what it CARRIES, never by its name.
- Nested trees are children of ONE `scope.eval`. The called fold of a nesting type refuses by name; the
  exported `merge`/`emptyValue` bridge with one standalone evaluation per tree.
- Reports go on result SIBLINGS (`undeclared`, `deprecations`), never stderr: the eval cache swallows
  `trace`/`warn`, so a printed report appears once and never again.
- gen-merge computes the contribution FACT for warm reuse; gen-memo DECIDES reuse.
- Rows in the traps table are either a STANDING boundary (a deliberate divergence) or REMEDIATED (a
  defect now fixed). Never let a defect sit as an unmarked trap.
- Cite into `lib/` by SYMBOL, never by line range: a drifted range fails plausibly, while a stale symbol
  fails loudly.
- A single-caller helper lives in a `let` over its caller's lambda (file-level bindings cost a thunk per load).
- `lib/` is nixpkgs-free (purity cell); `ci/` uses nixpkgs as the equivalence oracle's reference side.

**Working in it:** `nix develop ./ci --command ci`, `... ci --tests-error`, `... ci --tests-process`
(per-process cells), `bash ci/modules-sh-ratchet.sh`; CI runs `nix flake check ./ci` then `nix fmt -- --ci`.
The `types` half of the drift check moves with the locked gen-types, with no gen-merge commit.

**Traps (standing boundaries):**

---
name: arms-that-should-not-be-offered
description: When an option in a design fork regresses behaviour the reference implementation supports, depends on changing an upstream you do not control, or hinges on an unmeasured fact.
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Do not offer as acceptable an arm that refuses what the reference system serves, or an arm
that needs the upstream to change. Treat the first as a smell to root-cause; mark the second
foreclosed. When arms hinge on an unmeasured fact, the right new arm is "measure first".

**Why:**

- Context: gen re-implements the nixpkgs module system (gen-merge and friends), with evaluation
  parity against nixpkgs as a core objective. A proposal priced "cells refused where the upstream serves" as an acceptable
  shortfall. Owner: "anywhere that's true has a significant smell; we need to step back and look at
  why, regardless of past rulings." A rarity exemption was proposed and rejected: a census proves
  presence, not absence, so "rare" cannot be established.
- An arm requiring a patch to the upstream library was recommended as "the only measured arm that
  meets both conditions". Owner: "impossible, we can't change it." Parity has to hold against releases
  already shipped, and upstream acceptance is outside your control.
- A parity question depended on WHERE a check was dropped (the upstream's own evaluation, or the
  re-implementation calling an upstream function). That was unmeasured. The owner took "measure first";
  a scout split the cells by class and the ruling followed the split.

**How to apply:**

- Before putting an arm whose price includes a regression against the reference: name the mechanism
  forcing it, look for the construction arm (thread the value, re-home it, fix the walk), and audit the
  ruling that forbids serving. Put the root-cause arm and a scout, not the shortfall. Challenge a past
  ruling if it is provably a design defect.
- Landing rules that came with this: a landing does not regress a working cell; a landing that only
  moves cells up the severity ladder (abort to refusal to value, silent to loud) may land; order work
  by severity, then positive evidence of presence.
- Upstream-change arms: list as foreclosed with the reason. Look for your side's form of the same
  mechanism. An upstream patch can still be useful as a MEASUREMENT of where the theory puts the door.
- Parity is not value-identity. Read the actual criterion's clauses, find the fact that decides which
  applies, and establish it (a spy that throws plus `--show-trace` usually settles it) before arms.
- Check whether an existing "refusal" ever enforced its check at all. In one case the check fired zero
  times.

Related: \[[before-asking-the-owner]\] \[[fix-the-producer-first]\]
Related: \[[presenting-a-decision]\] \[[before-asking-the-owner]\]

q18.query: Why might bash arrays and word splitting behave differently when running commands in zsh?

results.text:
---
name: zsh-is-not-bash
description: Applies when an agent harness runs shell commands under zsh (check `echo $ZSH_VERSION`) while the agent writes bash, including loop variable names and patterns.
type: trap
---

**Rule:** Check which shell actually runs your commands, then write for it. Under zsh: quote every
expansion, brace any expansion followed by `:` or `[` (`"${sha}:path"`, `"${b}[^:]*"`), use arrays
instead of word-splitting, never name a variable `path` or `status`, and read exit status unpiped.

**Why:** Measured differences:

Do not "fix" it by flipping the harness shell if existing docs instruct zsh idioms: in bash,
`$pipestatus` is simply unset, so every such exit check silently reads clean.

**How to apply:**

- `"${sha}:lib/x.nix"`; `"${b}[^:]*"`; `files=(a b c); grep -c foo "${files[@]}"`.
- Loop variables: `st`, `state`, `row`, `p`, `dir`. Never `path`, `status` or another tied/special name.
- Quote separator lines (`'====='`) or `setopt noequals`.
- Want a bash idiom? `bash -c '...'`.
- Read status unpiped: `cmd > out; echo $?`.
- The `path`, `:` and word-split forms fail silently; re-check output after any loop that uses a new
  variable name, and keep a live control in every sweep.

Related: \[[controls-for-absence-claims]\] \[[read-exit-status-unpiped]\]

| bash idiom                                                       | in zsh                                                                                                                                     | failure                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `${!var}`                                                        | unsupported; use `${(P)var}`                                                                                                               | loud: bad substitution                                                                                       |
| unquoted `$list` word-splits                                     | stays ONE word                                                                                                                             | SILENT: a sweep passed one concatenated path to grep and every count, including the positive control, read 0 |
| `$PIPESTATUS`                                                    | `$pipestatus` (lowercase)                                                                                                                  | silent empty                                                                                                 |
| `shopt`                                                          | `setopt`                                                                                                                                   | loud                                                                                                         |
| `"$sha:lib/x.nix"`                                               | `:l` (also `:h :t :r :e :s`) is a history modifier on `$sha` => `<sha>ib/x.nix`; this applies to `$var:` anywhere, not only git `rev:path` | SILENT: with `2>/dev/null`, `git show` returned 0 lines for every commit, a clean empty history scan         |
| assigning `path=...`                                             | `path` is a tied array bound to `PATH`; `cdpath`, `fpath`, `manpath`, `mailpath` likewise clobber their scalar twins                       | SILENT: every external command vanished; only `command not found` on stderr                                  |
| `for status in a b`                                              | `status` is read-only                                                                                                                      | loud: `read-only variable: status` (agents reach for it when iterating tracker statuses or exit codes)       |

---
name: reading-test-suite-output
description: When running, quoting or gating on a test command (nix-unit, flake check, just recipes), especially under zsh, and deciding whether a run was green
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Verify the runner before quoting a command, capture `2>&1` and the exit status
unpiped (only commit after seeing `exit=0`), and compare the collected count against the baseline you carried in. A green
summary and a zero failure count are not evidence on their own.

**Why (measured):**

- **A piped gate passes a red.** `nix-unit ... | tail -2 && git commit && git push` used `tail`'s
  status, 0: a failing suite committed and pushed a broken change to a public repo. The bash
  workaround `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is EMPTY under zsh (zsh spells it `$pipestatus`), and empty reads as
  success.
- **nix-unit moves its markers between streams depending on the outcome.** On a passing run,
  the ticks and `🎉 217/217` are on stdout and stderr is 0 bytes. On a failing run, stdout holds
  213 ticks with no ❌ and no summary, and stderr holds the ❌ lines and `213/217`. A
  stdout-only pipeline sees a failing run as success.
- **Three markers:** ✅, ❌ (mismatch) and ☢️ (evaluation error). A ❌-only grep undercounts.
- **A crashed run** looked like: exit 1, no summary line, zero ❌, zero ☢️, zero bytes of
  stderr, and 911 of 1153 cells collected. The only tells were the missing summary and the
  short count.
- **`N/N` can be an identity, not a check.** One runner computes `total = pass + fail`, so
  the two numbers match on any run that reaches the summary, including a truncated one.
- **Do not grep the diff renderer for a value.** It wraps values across padded columns, so
  both arms read 0. Assert the value as a cell and read ✅/❌.
- **A non-git copy of a test flake escapes its root.** Every gen-\* library's `ci/flake.nix` imports `../lib`; under
  a non-git path flake the root resolves to `ci/` and the import points elsewhere. Readings of
  15/864 and 7/486 were reported as catastrophic reds. Only the unmutated stock arm, which
  showed the identical 7/486, exposed it.
- **Repositories may have several test planes** (tests, error goldens, per-process cells).
  In gen-merge, `ci` alone read 816/816 while `ci --tests-error` read 328/471, and a build that
  ran two of three planes (missing `--tests-process`) landed a red main.
- **A recipe-listing grep missed parameterized `just` recipes** (`ci test="" *args:` has no
  colon after the name), and it reported real recipes as absent. Use `just -l` inside the
  devshell.

**How to apply:**

- Read the command from the repository's README and CI workflow, and list the test planes
  from the runner's own help. Every oracle names ALL planes.

- `cmd > out 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"` and then `tail -1 out`; do not chain `&&` off a piped verify. Count ✅, ❌ and ☢️, and compare the
  collected total to the expected baseline.

---
name: roles-common-protocol
description: The standing half every dispatched subagent role (scout, spec, gate, build) carries - measurement law, reporting disclosures, delivery and the stop protocol.
type: workflow
---

# Common protocol for every subagent role

## Measurement law

- **Every absence claim needs a positive control that FIRED**, same instrument, same run. A zero from
  a predicate that could not have matched is INVALID, not clean. See \[[controls-for-absence-claims]\].
- **Check a predicate's reach against the concept, not its spelling.** A true zero in the wrong
  library or under the wrong term produces a confident wrong conclusion.
- **Drive the check red and read it.** Produce the failing state and look at the output. Measured: a
  build whose edit silently wrote nothing returned `163/163` and its agent read that as success.
- **A probe whose two arms agree has measured nothing**, and neither has a one-armed probe compared
  with a figure from a document. Exhibit both arms from your own instrument, measuring the same object.
- **A report about an artefact is never a measurement of it.** Re-derive; do not relay.
- **Your brief is a claim set, not ground.** Briefs carried a false load-bearing claim in roughly half
  of sampled runs: either stale (true once, since fixed) or simply wrong (a count, path, cause).
  Test load-bearing claims before building on them. Emphasis marks protect nothing.
- **"At HEAD" is not a coordinate.** Re-derive any cited line, digest or path; say which copy you read;
  where a pin exists (lock file, store path, explicit sha) read the pinned revision.

## Shell facts that have caused false findings

- The tool named "Bash" may run zsh: unquoted `$list` does not word-split; `$pipestatus` not
  `$PIPESTATUS`; brace `"${sha}:path"` (zsh history modifiers otherwise mangle it and return nothing
  at exit 0); never name a variable `path` (it is tied to `PATH`). See \[[zsh-is-not-bash]\].
- Read exit status UNPIPED: `cmd > out; echo $?`. See \[[read-exit-status-unpiped]\].
- Do not `2>/dev/null` a measurement: it turns a missing tool into an absence finding.
- `grep -c` counts LINES; prose wraps. For phrases: `tr -s '[:space:]' ' ' | grep -o 'phrase' | wc -l`.
  Carry the unit (lines / occurrences / files) in every figure. See \[[grep-wrapper-and-count-units]\], \[[grep-wrapped-prose]\].
- `grep -r` does not follow symlinks; `-R` does.
- A test summary of `0/0` is a FALSE PASS. Check the collected count agrees with the summary.
  See \[[nix-unit-collection-traps]\].

## Control tokens

---
name: controls-for-absence-claims
description: When reporting a zero, an absence or an "identical" result, and building the positive/negative controls that make it meaningful
type: trap
verified: 2026-10-15; zsh 5.9.2, git 2.55.0
---

**Rule:** Every absence claim carries a positive control that runs YOUR predicate, in the same
instrument, same output form, same run and comparable complexity, on a case known to match. If the
control reads 0 too, the instrument is broken: fix it before reporting anything. Plant a positive if
the material has none, and mint fresh negative tokens each run.

**Why / measured:**

- Sweeps where every term AND the control read 0, each looking like a clean, well-controlled absence:
  zsh did not word-split an unquoted `$list`, so grep got one concatenated path; `git grep -lin` parsed
  as `--lin` and printed nothing to stdout; a tracker read failed with "database is busy" (rc 2) and
  produced empty output. The control is what exposed the first one.
- A sweep for pattern P was "controlled" by pattern Q firing 5 times. Both figures were true and the
  pairing proved nothing about P.
- P run against the very revision that "carried" the offending text returned 0, because the text had
  only ever existed in a report. When the corpus holds no known positive, a planted case is mandatory.
  Say that it was planted.
- Negative-control tokens get copied into reports and tracker bodies. A reused token later fires on the
  record of an earlier run and looks like a broken instrument. The opposite hazard follows: dismissing
  a genuine hit as "just a banked token".
- A control slug written into the file being swept makes the "MISSING" probe match the file's own
  documentation. The armed run then looks identical to a clean pass.
- A comparison instrument needs its own negative control. A nonexistent arm must report UNUSABLE, never
  IDENTICAL. The comparator can be dead while both subjects are fine.
- An id predicate also matches inside other records' text. Anchor it to the id field
  (`cut -f1 | grep -cx id`).
- A busy database read exited rc 2 with clean empty stdout (the error on stderr). Every grep over it read
  0, the positive control included; attempts 1 and 2 returned 0 lines, attempt 3 returned 3496. Killing
  a reader in flight hands its caller the same empty result. A "busy" error can also mean either live
  contention (a process holds the lock: wait) or a wedged store (no process: repair), with one text.
- Result rows prefixed with a status glyph made an id anchored at start-of-line (`grep -c '^<id>'`) read
  0 over a full result set. Print one real row before writing a predicate over a tool's output.
- In an aborting run no control can fire, because the abort destroys the output. The strongest form
  available is the same file and expressions at a size that returns. Say so explicitly.

**How to apply:**

| `"$b[^:]*"` in a pattern                                         | parsed as an array subscript                                                                                                               | loud: `bad math expression: operand expected at '^:'`                                                        |
| unquoted word starting with `=` (`echo =====`, a separator line) | `=cmd` expands to the path of `cmd` (EQUALS option)                                                                                        | loud but easy to misread: `zsh: ==== not found`, rc 1, the command never runs                                |

---
name: tracker-body-writes
description: When writing findings, rulings or obligations into an issue tracker (beads/br or similar) from a shell tool
type: practice
---

**Rule:** Write findings into the item's DESCRIPTION, not into comments or notes. Pass the
prose from a FILE, not as a command-line argument, and verify the stored text by reading it
back.

**Why:**

- Owner: "We don't use comments generally, we append directly to the body as nobody ever reads
  the comments." Comments were append-only (no edit or remove) and unread, so anything
  load-bearing there was invisible in practice. The body is what boots, gates, briefs and the
  agenda script read. Seven comments across six rows were written in one session despite the
  rule already being written down.
- Prose passed in zsh double quotes was mutated silently. A backticked control name was
  command-substituted away, leaving "live control ⇒ 9 same run" with the control unnamed.
  `visible ? key` was globbed and vanished (`zsh: no matches found: ?`). The tracker reported
  "appended 3675 chars", exit 0. The holes show only when you read the field back.
- `-d "<body>"` on a real body hit `Argument list too long`.
- An agenda script matched title and description only, so three forks banked in comments or
  notes read 0.

**How to apply:**

- Read the current body, append a dated block, and write the whole body back with
  `--description-file <path>`. A shrink below half the current length needs `--force`: that
  guard is deliberate, so think before using it.
- Use a wrapper that reads the payload from disk and refuses on an empty payload, an empty
  current body, or a read-back that is not byte-identical.
- Write the payload with a file-writing tool, not a shell heredoc.
- Where an argument is unavoidable (a short title, a `--reason`), SINGLE-quote it. Single
  quotes are literal in zsh.
- Model-facing commands use native text output (\[[json-for-programs-text-for-models]\]).
- After banking, run the deriving query (agenda, ready list) and confirm the row appears.
- Bodies are self-contained: markdown outside the tracker does not survive compaction, and the
  graph does.

Related: \[[durable-records-not-handoffs]\] \[[filing-caps]\]

---
name: redirect-truncates-before-read
description: When a read-modify-write script rebuilds a file from a tool's output
type: trap
verified: 2026-10-15; zsh 5.9.2
---

**Rule:** Gate every whole-file replacement on the intermediate being non-empty: `test -s body.md || { echo ABORT; exit 1; }`.

**Why:** `>` truncates the file before the command runs. In a near miss, the idiom `tool read > body.md; cat >> body.md <<'EOF' ...; tool write --from body.md` ran after a `cd` that broke the tool's workspace lookup. The read failed loudly, but `body.md` was already empty, so the append left only the new block. That file would have replaced a 38 KB record with 4 KB. The write failed only because it hit the same broken lookup. Re-running from the right directory to "fix" the visible error would have gone through and destroyed the record.

The loud failure and the destructive one are different events, and the loud one is not guaranteed to come first. The last command's exit code says nothing about whether the first stage produced its output.

**How to apply:**

- Check the read's exit status and that its output is non-empty before appending.
- A store whose write REPLACES a whole record makes every append a read-modify-write. The read is
  non-deterministic under load: a read of a 454-line record returned the literal one-line string `null`
  (an accessor over an empty result), and the next read seconds later returned all 454. Read twice and
  refuse if either read is empty or `null` or the two differ; do not refuse on a fixed minimum length,
  since short records are legitimate.
- Verify by checksum of the preserved prefix after the write (`head -n <old line count> | md5sum`), never
  by line count: a truncated record plus a long block can have more lines than before.
- A store's own length guard refusing your write is a measurement that your read was short. Re-read;
  never answer it with a force flag, which turns a bad read into a lost record.
- Prefer a helper script that refuses on an empty payload, an empty current body, or a read-back that is not byte-identical to what was written.
- Prefer the editor or Write tool for generated files. Unlike a redirect, it refuses when the target changed underneath you.

Supersedes the general half of br-description-replace-is-read-modify-write (retired with the tracker-specific traps).

Related: \[[read-exit-status-unpiped]\] \[[controls-for-absence-claims]\]
